program: Improv Undergrad STEM Ed(IUSE), EHR CL Opportunities (NSF 14-302), UNDERGRADUATE EDUCATION
projectOutComesReport:
This project explored how computer vision-based biomechanics can be applied to improve education, with a particular focus on creating learning applications that transform the way undergraduate students engage with data science. The central achievement of the project was the development of innovative mobile apps that use students’ own body motions as data sources. By capturing movements such as walking, standing, or jumping, the apps enabled students to interact directly with their own data to learn complex topics in biomechanics and data analytics. Through this experiential approach, abstract concepts such as principal component analysis and clustering became more tangible, intuitive, and engaging. Surveys of undergraduate students confirmed that this method not only improved their understanding but also increased their enthusiasm for learning data science.

The development of these apps represented an important contribution to the field of STEM education. Traditional data science instruction often relies on pre-existing datasets, which can feel disconnected from students’ experiences. By contrast, the apps created in this project allowed learners to generate and analyze their own motion data in real time, creating a personalized and active learning environment. This approach broadened access to data science by making knowledge more approachable for students without prior technical backgrounds, and it supported the broader mission of enhancing undergraduate education through innovative pedagogy. Both apps have been published in peer-reviewed journals and made freely available for download, ensuring that educators and students nationwide can benefit from them.

While the primary emphasis of the project was on education, the research also explored how computer vision algorithms can contribute to other domains. For example, the project examined preliminary methods for automating safety assessments in workplace environments, where manual evaluation of lifting tasks is still common practice. Early studies demonstrated that computer vision-based assessments can produce results comparable to those of safety professionals, showing potential for reducing the time and effort currently required for such evaluations. These findings indicate that the educational tools and underlying algorithms developed in this project could extend beyond the classroom to address broader societal needs, including workplace safety and healthcare applications.

The broader impacts of this work are multifaceted. The open-access apps have been used not only in undergraduate courses but also in outreach activities such as lab tours and K-12 summer camps. These activities introduced younger learners to the connections between data, movement, and technology, helping to spark early interest in STEM careers. The research also contributed to the academic community through publications, conference presentations, and engagement with educators in biomechanics and data science who provided input to refine the apps and improve their content flow.

In summary, this project demonstrated how computer vision and biomechanics can be harnessed to transform the way students learn data science. The creation of interactive, motion-based learning apps provided a new model for experiential education that improves comprehension and engagement, while also offering pathways for broader applications in safety and health. By making the apps and source code openly available, the project supports long-term sustainability and continued innovation. The outcomes highlight the power of integrating emerging technologies into education to prepare the next generation of students for a data-driven future.

abstractText:
Science provides an extraordinarily powerful tool for investigating nature, and nature supplies an
endless abundance of research topics that are ripe for scientists to investigate. Faced with such
abundance, scientists must regularly choose where to place their efforts: which questions to pursue and
which to leave for another day, which results to prepare for publication and which to set aside, and so
on. When making these decisions, researchers face incentives that scientific funders and scientific
journals create through the peer‐review processes that funders and journals use to ensure quality and
rigor in the science they support and publish. Yet we understand very little about how the incentives
created by peer‐review in scientific funding and publication shape the scientific activity of individual
investigators, and how those decisions scale up to impact the aggregate knowledge that science creates.
In this project, we will develop new mathematical theory to understand how incentives created by
scientific funders and journals affect individual scientific activity and the subsequent production of
scientific knowledge. This theory will provide a foundation for evaluating proposed refinements of
funding or publication practices, and for understanding whether these changes will nudge the scientific
enterprise towards a more reliable and expansive understanding of the natural world.

We will focus on two questions. First, how do journals' publication decisions shape the ability of their
readership to learn from the scientific literature? Second, how do the incentives created by funding and
publication structures motivate scientists to work on certain projects and shy away from others? For
each question, we will ask how peer‐review filters function differently for basic versus applied research.
We will investigate these questions by building and analyzing mathematical models that incorporate
elements of information theory, economics, forecasting assessment, and statistics. In the long run, this
work will deepen our understanding of science as a social process by revealing how scientific institutions
generate incentives that shape the direction of scientific inquiry. More immediately, it will provide a
theoretical framework to explore how possible changes to the peer‐review process such as registered
reports or pre‐print servers may change scientists' collective process of learning and discovery. Finally,
we will develop an online module to help readers become savvier consumers of the scientific literature,
and we will share our findings with the editorial board of a leading biological journal.

jrnl.auth: Gross, Kevin and Bergstrom, Carl T.
jrnl.jrnlTitl: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

orgLongName: Directorate for Social, Behavioral and Economic Sciences
orgLongName2: SBE Office of Multidisciplinary Activities
program: SCIENCE OF SCIENCE POLICY
projectOutComesReport:
Science is a human endeavor. Broadly, our work helps to understand how the norms and institutions of science influence the decisions that scientists make when developing their research programs. Those decisions in turn shape the knowledge that scientists produce. By unpacking the incentives that scientific norms and institutions create, we build a more robust and expansive understanding of why scientific knowledge is largely reliable. Our work also identifies how potential nudges to the scientific process might shift scientific activity, and generates predictions about how those shifts will affect scientific productivity.

In this project, we have specifically examined how several integral components of contemporary science impact researchers? willingness to take on scientific risks. In science, the safest research programs---in the sense that they are most likely to yield publishable results---are probably not the most productive ones. Several lines of evidence suggest that many of the most important breakthroughs arise when scientists take risks, pursuing lines of research that have a high likelihood of failing entirely, but that will pay rich dividends should they succeed. Researchers and funders alike are concerned that too many impediments stand in the way of high-risk, high-reward science.

One such impediment is a consequence of the peer-review system that is central to scientific activity. Many projects are reviewed at multiple stages: before the work is done (ex ante) to determine if the study is worth funding, and after the work is done (ex post) to determine if the results are worth publishing. Using mathematical models of the scientific process, we find that ex ante peer review discourages risky research because reviewers tend to expect that risky studies are unlikely to be successful, whereas with ex post review the outcome of the research is already known. The tension between projects that are most likely to survive ex ante review versus those that are most likely to survive ex post review is a major dynamic that shapes contemporary scientific activity. Our theory thus suggests why grant proposals inevitably seem more risk averse than results presented in top-tier journals, and sounds a note of caution about how ex ante peer review of journal publications might shift scientific activity. Separately, this work also suggests why convening grant reviewers as a panel is especially important for supporting research that has the potential to resolve scientific controversies.

Another impediment involves the way that scientists are rewarded for their labor. Because it is difficult for the scientific community to monitor the effort that researchers put into their projects and the scientific risk that they take on, the community indirectly incentivizes effort and risk-taking by rewarding researchers for the results that they generate.  We have developed mathematical models to explore the consequences of this fact on scientists? willingness to take scientific risks.  These models suggest that incentives for hard work cannot be perfectly aligned with incentives for scientific risk-taking. Thus, because researchers are unwilling to stake their livelihoods on the vicissitudes of scientific chance, they choose safer projects than would be optimal to maximize the rate of scientific discovery. This work reveals an additional reason why funding programs designed to foster risky research often fail to attract proposals for high-risk, high-return science.

abstractText:
Sensory feedback from moving legs is critical for functional and dynamically stable locomotion. Although it is clear that motion-related sensory feedback influences inter-leg coordination and selection of gaits (walking, trotting, galloping, etc.), it is not known which sensory modalities (e.g., muscle length- or force-related signals) and sources of feedback (e.g., hip or knee muscles) mediate these locomotor changes. Therefore, this project aims to understand how sensory neurons providing information about the length of hip muscles regulate interlimb coordination and gait selection. This goal will be accomplished by selectively and reversibly stimulating these sensory neurons in an intelligent, closed-loop, and well-controlled manner. This project will lead to the development of new neural implant tools and associated computational algorithms for an in-vivo manipulation of motion-related sensory signals in a large animal model, the cat. The new findings of this project and the developed methods will substantially enhance our understanding of the mechanisms of sensory locomotor control and contribute to developing novel therapeutic interventions. The proposed multidisciplinary research approaches will also significantly expand the utility and capabilities of the rapidly growing field of optogenetics, enabling transformative research and providing unprecedented new experimental tools for neuroscience. The most noticeable long-term benefits of this work to society will be an improvement in the quality of life for a sizable population of people affected by a wide range of movement deficits, from limb loss to sensory neuropathy. These individuals will benefit from the development of neural interfaces between the nervous and engineering systems controlled by machine learning algorithms. Throughout this project, efforts will be made to recruit and train graduate and undergraduate students from underrepresented groups. Outreach activities will also be organized to share resources, tools, and knowledge with teachers, students, and underrepresented groups. The results of the proposed research and educational activities will be shared with students, scientific communities, and the public through science fairs, publications, workshops, conferences, and the Internet.

The overall goal of this proposal is to characterize the mechanisms of somatosensory control of interlimb coordination and gait selection by spindle afferents of hip muscles in the cat model by developing and utilizing in-vivo an intelligent and closed-loop optoelectronic neural interface system. In particular, in this proposal high-density, efficient, and wirelessly-powered implantable opto-electro (WIOE) neural interface devices will be developed. Each WIOE heterogeneously incorporates an optoelectronic array of 64 transparent microelectrodes and 16 microscale light-emitting-diodes (µLEDs), a system-on-a-chip (SoC), and a power receiver (Rx) coil in an mm3-size package, capable of optogenetic stimulation and electrical recording of neural activities. Wireless telemetry links will be implemented for efficient transcutaneous power and wideband data transmission between an external data-acquisition/control unit and the distributed array of WIOE implants. Multiple WIOE devices will be implanted in selected dorsal root ganglia (DRG) of the cat. Neural activities of DRG neurons, EMG activities of selected muscles of the four limbs, and full-body locomotor kinematics will be recorded, and spindle afferent activities will be manipulated via optogenetic stimulation in selected DRGs during unconstrained cat locomotion. Machine learning (ML) models leveraging the spatiotemporal structures in the signals and mapping afferent  activities in DRGs to limb kinematics will be applied for achieving closed-loop control of the optogenetic  neuromodulation. The proposed research activities will be conducted by a team of collaborators with complementary research expertise in the areas of bioMEMS, wireless microelectronics, machine learning, artificial intelligence, and behavioral neuroscience. The successful development of the proposed intelligent and closed-loop optoelectronic neural interface will yield a robust building block for a comprehensive set of minimally invasive neural interfaces to study somatosensory control of movement, as well as monitor or treat somatosensory pathological conditions.

abstractText:
North Carolina State University (NCSU) will establish the Learning Analytics in STEM Education Research (LASER) Institute to build learning analytics capacity in STEM education research. The institute will provide professional development for early and mid-career STEM education researchers in learning analytics, a computational research methodology. The goal of the institute is to increase the capacity of researchers to understand and improve STEM learning and learning environments through the use of new sources of data and analytical approaches. The institute will be anchored by a week-long intensive training program consisting of hands-on learning labs, presentations from experts in the field, support for research planning and data analyses, and opportunities for networking and collaboration. In addition, follow up support will occur throughout the year.

The institute will prepare STEM education research scholars to: 1) understand the methodologies, applications, and ethical issues of learning analytics as these relate to understanding and improving STEM education, 2) gain proficiency in R, a free software environment applied to computational analysis techniques (e.g., network analysis, text mining, machine learning, and data dashboards) using real-world STEM education data, and 3) expand professional networks in support of STEM education research efforts. 

This research institute is funded by ECR (the core research program of the Education and Human Resources directorate) and attends specifically to critical aspects in research capacity building.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

program: Capacity-Building Projects
projectOutComesReport:
Program Overview

The Learning Analytics in STEM Education Research (LASER) Institute addressed the growing demand for advanced research methodologies in STEM education. By equipping early and mid-career scholars with the tools and knowledge to leverage learning analytics (LA), the LASER Institute empowered researchers to examine and improve STEM learning environments. Spanning three cohorts from 2020 to 2023, this initiative directly impacted 142 researchers from institutions across 30 states and 7 countries, while prioritizing scholars from underrepresented groups and minority-serving institutions to broaden participation in STEM education research.

The LASER Institute was a year-long professional development program, featuring an intensive summer workshop and a sustained online community of practice. During the five-day summer workshops, scholars engaged in foundational and advanced learning labs covering topics such as machine learning, text mining, social network analysis, and data visualization using R. These workshops were complemented by webinars, office hours, and collaborative activities during the academic year, fostering an inclusive and supportive network of scholars. The program’s adaptability over its three-year duration ensured that scholars with diverse technical backgrounds could fully engage with the curriculum.

Intellectual Merit

The LASER Institute made significant contributions to the intellectual advancement of STEM education research. Scholars reported marked improvements in their ability to apply computational techniques to complex educational challenges. Participants developed research projects that utilized text mining to analyze qualitative data from educational institutions, employed machine learning to predict student retention, and applied social network analysis to explore collaboration patterns in online learning environments.

Scholars produced a comprehensive range of academic outputs that they attributed to their participation in LASER. Collectively, scholars reported over 80 academic products including, but are not limited to: 30 conference presentations and proceedings; 21 published journal articles, book chapters or books; 13 workshops, symposia, or service activities; 11 manuscripts in progress; 9 funded grants awarded and 6 submitted. This productivity underscored the program’s success in equipping participants with the technical and conceptual tools necessary to conduct impactful research and address pressing educational challenges.

Broader Impacts

The LASER Institute’s societal impacts are evident in its commitment to broadening participation in STEM education research. Across all three cohorts, the program recruited 142 scholars from a pool of 731 applicants, achieving a scholar demographic profile that reflects a strong commitment to diversity. Among scholars, approximately 72% were women and 57% came from minority racial and ethnic groups. Additionally, 21% of scholars were affiliated with minority-serving institutions. These efforts significantly exceeded national benchmarks for diversity in STEM fields and directly supported NSF’s goal of broadening participation among underrepresented groups.

Participants also applied their training to improve learning environments for diverse populations. LASER alumni developed tools to analyze equity gaps in STEM education, informed institutional decision-making through data analytics, and applied their skills to mentoring students and designing inclusive curricula. The Institute’s emphasis on actionable research, as well as an innovative grant program implemented in the final year, helped ensure that scholars not only advanced their careers but also contributed to systemic improvements in STEM education.

The program’s legacy extends beyond individual participants through the creation of a sustainable research infrastructure. LASER’s open-access curriculum, hosted on GitHub, includes comprehensive instructional modules made up of conceptual overviews, code-alongs, interactive case studies, essential readings, and assessment activities. These repositories provide an enduring resource for researchers worldwide. Additionally, the adoption of LASER’s methodologies and resources within participating universities and institutions ensures the program’s impact will continue for years to come.

Commitment to Excellence

LASER’s success was driven by a commitment to continuous improvement. Each year, the program refined its selection criteria, workshop structure, and curriculum based on participant feedback and evaluation. Recognizing the diversity in participants’ technical skills, LASER provided differentiated learning paths and enhanced scaffolding to support both novice and advanced users. These adaptations ensured scholars from varied backgrounds could succeed and benefit from the program. The Institute also reduced technical barriers by improving documentation, integrating cutting-edge tools like large language models, and offering extensive individual support.

The program’s emphasis on community-building further strengthened its outcomes. Scholars reported high levels of satisfaction with the Institute’s supportive and collaborative environment. Networking activities and research goal-setting sessions enabled participants to form meaningful professional connections and establish long-term research partnerships. These efforts created a vibrant scholarly community that continues to drive innovation and collaboration in STEM education research.

Conclusion

The LASER Institute represents a transformative model for capacity-building in STEM education research. By advancing scholars’ technical expertise, fostering diversity, and promoting actionable research, the program has made lasting contributions to both the intellectual and societal dimensions of STEM education. Its legacy is evident in the productive research careers of its participants, the enduring resources it has created, and the systemic improvements it has inspired. LASER’s achievements underscore the critical role of targeted professional development in shaping the future of STEM education and research.

abstractText:
This project will determine how soils and soil organisms respond to severe drought, a condition that will be more common in the future, and how this response will impact the global carbon cycle. The increasing frequency of drought due to changing rainfall patterns is threatening the world's ecosystems and food security. Rainfall frequency also can affect whether the immense amount of carbon present in soil stays there, or is emitted by soil microbes into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide (CO2). In order to accurately predict the impact of drought on soils, soil microbes and the carbon cycle, this project will use samples from the Drought-Net Research Coordination Network supported by NSF.  Drought-Net consists of a series of simple, inexpensive experiments that control rainfall at over 150 plots of land worldwide using the same standard protocols. Soil samples from 39 Drought-Net sites that have been exposed to drought for four years will be manipulated in the laboratory to determine how they respond to different amounts of moisture. Soil microbial community changes and CO2 emission will be measured, and the results will be incorporated into computer models of global carbon cycling. These models can then predict how drought will cause changes and feedbacks in carbon cycling and, in turn, ecosystem function and stability. The studies will also involve training at of postdoctoral researchers, graduate and undergraduate students, and other educational and outreach activities. Successful completion of the goals and objectives of this project will help society understand how it needs to adapt and respond to global environmental change. 

While the recent inclusion of microbial mechanisms in ecosystem models has improved our ability to predict soil carbon (C) cycling, even the most advanced of these models explains only 50% of the variation in current C pools, leaving little confidence in projections of future soil C stocks. Past efforts have mainly focused on microbial temperature responses, but moisture and drought may be an even more important constraint on microbial activity. Thus, an understanding of microbial moisture responses is required to improve ecosystem C models. This research addresses four key questions: (1) what drives differences in moisture response functions across ecosystems? (2) how does severe drought alter moisture response across ecosystems? (3) what microbial mechanisms influence differences in moisture response functions? (4) what are the implications of different moisture responses for C storage? In order to build a robust predictive framework for soil microbial moisture functions, this project will leverage the Drought-Net Research Coordination Network, which has implemented standardized, coordinated rainfall manipulation experiments across the world. Intact soil cores from ambient and drought treatments at 39 sites will be exposed to a range of soil water potentials to quantify how the moisture response of heterotrophic respiration depends on historical climate and soil factors. Underlying microbial mechanisms will be examined by characterizing physiological traits and tolerances at individual and community levels. Results will be scaled to the ecosystem level by first testing how aggregated community responses influence function in a trait-based model, and then by incorporating response functions into conventional and microbially-explicit ecosystem models of soil C cycling.

Project findings

Soils hold a large amount of carbon. As part of the natural carbon cycle (“decomposition”), microbes in the soil respire this carbon as CO2 into the atmosphere. How fast this process occurs depends on how much water is in the soil, but our ability to predict the relationship between the amount of moisture and the amount of respiration is poor. We challenged the prevailing assumption that soil respiration depends solely on current conditions, and tested whether historical rainfall patterns had shaped this ecosystem function. Because microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) are responsible for soil respiration and decomposition, we further hypothesized that the types of microbes present, and whether they are sensitive or tolerant to drought, might help us understand this relationship between soil water and respiration rate. We also expect that an improved understanding of these processes would help predict how much respiration would occur in the future, given expectations for more severe drought. The problem is that biologists are only just beginning to uncover the basics about how microbiomes vary across the world, adapt to new conditions, and what characteristics help them under low or high water conditions.  

 

We sampled sites from all over the world to capture many different environments and soil microbiomes (Figure 1). Each site we sampled included plots that were exposed to normal rainfall or had undergone an experimental extreme drought for 4-6 years. In the lab, we added water to these soils to create a range of very dry to very wet conditions, and analyzed how much each soil respired and how the microbiomes changed based on their site of origin and rainfall treatment. We first overturned a dominant paradigm – that all sites and ecosystems would respond the same; in contrast, we showed that the relationship between soil water and respiration differed in each site, which might explain why it is challenging to predict this with just one function for all sites. Furthermore, we demonstrated that these effects persisted through multiple years of extreme drought, suggesting that any shifts in response to new conditions are likely to be very slow. Microbial communities – previously thought to be roughly equal in their ability to respond to drought – also differed. In particular, we discovered many unique strategies by which microbes from different sites tolerate drought, as opposed to all responding in a single manner (e.g., to go dormant) for all sites. Our results suggest that the abundance of these characteristics, or traits, or microbial communities, do influence the amount of carbon each soil will respire as water becomes more or less available, and using this biology in ecosystem models could help us predict how ecosystem carbon balance will change as climates and soils change in the future.

 

The results of this work will enable improvements to ecosystem models that can better project expected future conditions. Since a rapid release of carbon from soils could create positive feedback with climate change, these projections are especially important, and help fine-tune goals for emission reductions and other mitigation strategies. Through this project we also trained four women postdoctoral scientists (Bachega, Broderick, Chavez, Rocca), and two women technicians (VanderStel, Harrell). We also generated a large dataset that can be used for site-specific analyses and future synthesis, amplifying our impact on personnel.

 

Other products

All data generated from the project will be uploaded to public repositories, including Dryad (respiration and site data) and the NCBI Short Read Archive (microbial data).

 

Anticipated publications

We have the following manuscripts currently in preparation:

Bachega L, Chavez L, DroughtNet Consortium, Evans SE, Allison SD, Hawkes CV. Seasonality and aridity constrain how soil respiration responds to moisture at global scale.

 

Bachega L, DroughtNet Consortium, Allison SD, Evans SE, Hawkes CV. A comparison of respiration responses to moisture in intact cores and homogenized soils.

 

Broderick, C, DroughtNet Consortium, Allison SD, Hawkes CV, Evans SE. Microbial gene expression underlying the respiration moisture response curve.

abstractText:
A technology that can reduce the friction or drag on ship hulls would have a substantial economic and environmental impact by improving fuel efficiency. Microstructured superhydrophobic surfaces may retain air pockets that can act as gas lubrication between the water and the ship hull. Although the superhydrophobic surfaces have been studied for nearly two decades, it is only recently that periodic linear-trench structures have been shown to be effective for marine crafts traveling in open water, which represents sea, oceans, and lakes. The manufacturing of such well-defined micro-trenches has relied on silicon-based microfabrication based on semiconductor manufacturing approaches. These silicon processes are prohibitively expensive and not scalable for large surface areas, such as ship hulls. To address these challenges, a team from North Carolina State University and University of California at Los Angeles would like to utilize roll coating methodology, which is well known for cost-effective and large-scale production, to form the periodic microstructures on large substrates. This new process is researched to develop friction-reduction coatings for ship hulls and study their physical and chemical durability. Hence, outcomes from this research will benefit a wide array of marine applications, including commercial and military ships, which play a significant role in the national and global economies and security applications. 

This project is investigates the spontaneous pattern generation by ribbing on polymer surfaces during roll coating in an ordered manner using a fundamentally new approach to manufacture three-dimensional micro and nano-scale structures on a large-area substrate. The objectives are to establish the scientific foundation to control the microstructures formed during the roll coating, and to fabricate and validate the drag reduction efficiency of the surfaces in realistic flow conditions of open water and Reynolds number greater than 1 million. The research team will utilize computational modeling to predict the deformation behavior of the viscoelastic polymer verified by the experimental observations. For the proof-of-concept of drag reduction in realistic flows, a microstructured film and a smooth film will be layered on the bottom of a motorboat specifically outfitted to reliably compare the fluid shear stresses on the two. This project will educate the next generation of engineers and scientists through multidisciplinary research involving manufacturing, materials science, computational modeling, and fluid mechanics. The research outcome will be also used to educate K-12, undergraduate, as well as graduate-level students through various formats such as outreach activities and innovative curricular efforts.

projectOutComesReport:
The objective of this research is to understand the roll-coating process for creating micro-/nano-scale 3D ribbed features on viscoelastic materials reinforced with carbon nanotubes (CNTs). This study aims to develop advanced multifunctional nanocomposite materials with significantly improved behavior, such as super-hydrophobicity, hydrodynamic drag reduction, and high strain-rate damage tolerance. We utilized a combination of experimental methods and computational modeling to analyze how process parameters influence the surface ribbing microstructures. Our findings have been disseminated through nine journal papers and one peer-reviewed conference paper to the manufacturing and material research communities.

Key results from this project include the demonstration of a simple, template-free roll-coating technique to fabricate periodic microstructures by shearing viscoelastic composite materials. The CNT-polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) composites enabled controllable semi-linear ribbing with periodicities ranging from 100s µm, effectively reducing drag. We found that the pressure gradient (dp/dx) of the flow direction significantly affects ribbing instability behavior, and that it can be adjusted through roller gap (or film thickness) and roller speed. Additionally, we developed multi-layer composite films exhibiting a radiative cooling power of 39.1 W/m², achieving high infrared absorption/emission (97%), UV-visible reflectivity (96%), and dirt-resistance.

Furthermore, we validated a computational model, based on a dynamic finite-element (FE) approach  for the symmetric forward-roll coating process of CNT-PDMS thin films, which allowed us to predict and control ribbing microstructures during large-scale rolling. By examining roller gap, rotational speed, and CNT content, we identified critical parameters governing ribbing instabilities, facilitating the design of multifunctional surfaces with properties such as drag reduction, anti-biofouling, superhydrophobicity, and anti-icing. We also investigated the thermomechanical behavior of ribbed thin films under high strain rates for aerospace and defense applications. Additionally, we characterized and modeled the large-strain mechanical behavior and microstructure of CNT-PDMS thin films, focusing on the effects of CNT loading, agglomeration, distribution, and orientation on mechanical performance and fracture behavior. This comprehensive approach allowed for precise control over ribbed and non-ribbed structures, enhancing their surface functionalities and performance across various applications.

 

The broader impacts of this project are evident in the numerous education and career opportunities created for both undergraduate and graduate students. Four Ph.D. students successfully completed their dissertations as part of this research, significantly advancing their academic and professional careers. Additionally, several undergraduate and master’s students engaged in research related to this project, gaining invaluable hands-on laboratory experience and the opportunity to present their findings at conferences. Ph.D. graduates from this effort have scientific staff positions in National Laboratories, such as Los Alamos National Laboratory, and leading corporate research centers, such as Intel.

Beyond individual student development, this project contributes to the engineering research community by fostering collaboration across disciplines and enhancing knowledge transfer between academia and industry. By addressing real-world challenges through innovative research, we are not only preparing the next generation of engineers but also promoting the application of cutting-edge technologies in various sectors. This engagement helps cultivate a skilled workforce ready to tackle pressing engineering challenges, ultimately benefiting society at large.

abstractText:
Cloud computing frameworks enable a wide range of services while sharing computation resources and infrastructure costs. To achieve these benefits, cloud computing frameworks rely on layers of abstractions to reduce the complexity of distributed and heterogeneous computational infrastructure. Abstractions hide resource management complexities and improve programmability. However, abstractions make cloud frameworks less observable, resulting in various forms of inefficiencies. This project will address the challenges of practical cloud monitoring techniques to guide cloud application development and system design.

This project will explore the inefficiency patterns in cloud computing infrastructures and applications. More specifically, it will provide novel measurement techniques to enable monitoring these inefficiencies across the cloud layers of abstraction. Additionally, the project will develop tools that will provide actionable insights for high-performance cloud frameworks and application development. This project has three thrusts. First, it will measure language-level abstractions for intra-application inefficiencies. Second, it will explore the inefficient communication patterns among microservices for inter-service optimization. Third, it will develop tools to analyze inefficiencies in the entire stack of cloud software layers of abstraction.

This project will bridge the knowledge gap between application developers and system designers to provide more efficient cloud environments. It will advance the state-of-the-art cloud monitoring techniques and address the current and future challenges in the cloud computing community. The tools developed from this project will have broad interest from industry, research institutes, and laboratories for efficient code execution and high system throughput. Furthermore, the project will disseminate the obtained knowledge through hands-on training sessions and tutorials. Finally, the project will facilitate curriculum development with a particular focus on involving minority and under-represented students.

The project will maintain a website at https://www.probir.info/cloudprof. The website will host all the project outcomes, including the publications, open-source code, toolkits, datasets, documentation, and tutorials. The website will be accessible to the public throughout the project lifetime and beyond.

projectOutComesReport:
he project "Towards Efficient Cloud Services" achieved significant
outcomes, aligning with its intellectual merit and broader impacts.


Intellectual Merit:

The project introduced three key innovations:

1. Novel Measurement Techniques: We developed advanced profiling tools
that target mainstream languages, architectures, and workloads. For
the languages, we support Java and Python, together with native
libraries, which are common in cloud workloads. For the architectures,
we target both CPUs and GPUs. For workloads, we mainly study deep
learning applications, and other data analytics workloads.

2. Actionable Insights: Using the developed tools, we identified and
addressed common inefficiencies in cloud software stacks. We
identified inefficiencies in Python and Java codes, as well as their
interactions with native libraries. The insights are actionable, which
lead to nontrivial speedups by removing unnecessary computation,
replacing with a lightweight API, and avoiding memory bloat.

3. Practical Applicability: The tools developed during this project,
including DrPy, ValueExpert, OJXPerf, were released as open-source
software, ensuring ongoing use and improvement by the community. These
tools are practical solutions that can be applied across various cloud
environments, benefiting developers and researchers.


Broader Impacts:

The broader impacts of the project are substantial and wide-ranging:

1. Educational Contributions: The project was integrated into academic
curricula, providing hands-on training for students in cloud computing
and system performance. Students were actively involved in the
research, co-authoring papers, and gaining practical skills in
performance optimization. This hands-on experience has equipped future
engineers and researchers with the expertise needed to tackle
real-world performance challenges.

2. Widespread Adoption and Collaboration: The open-source nature of
the developed tools has ensured accessibility for a wide range of
users, including industry, research institutes, and Department of
Energy (DoE) laboratories. The practical benefits of tools like
ValueExpert and EasyView have sparked interest from these sectors,
fostering collaboration and further research into efficient cloud
services.

3. Enhanced System Performance: The tools and findings from this
project will lead to improved cloud service performance, reducing
latency and resource consumption. By enhancing the efficiency of cloud
applications, this project supports more sustainable and eco-friendly
computing practices, addressing concerns about the environmental
impact of large-scale data centers.

In summary, this project has delivered innovative tools and techniques
that improve cloud service performance, offer practical insights, and
promote broader educational and industry collaboration. The outcomes
have set the stage for future advancements in cloud computing
efficiency.

abstractText:
Many complex structures that arise in nature are perceived globally as continuous objects, although at the microscopic level they emerge from certain laws that appear to be discrete. What the relation is between the discrete and continuous "worlds", how one impacts the other, and what laws they obey are the fundamental questions that the PI intends to investigate. This project focuses on the Hamming cube, the simplest discrete object that consists of binary strings of given length and that can encode any complex information. As the complexity of the information increases, the lengths of the encoded strings increase exponentially. The goal of the project is to develop mathematics on the Hamming cube that would allow us to encode the structures of the continuous world into the discrete world, and vice versa. The new techniques developed could have surprising applications in complexity theory as well as classical and quantum algorithms. Many of these problems are accessible to students and this project aims to continue the PI's work with undergraduate and graduate students in this area.
 
This project will consider a series of problems in the Gauss space and, most importantly, in its discrete counterpart, the Hamming cube. Unlike the classical case of the unit circle, many fundamental questions of Fourier analytic type are still open for the Hamming cube due to its unique discrete geometric structure. The first and main direction of the proposal is to resolve Weissler's conjecture, an old open problem in complex hypercontractivity theory on the Boolean cube that gives necessary and sufficient conditions for boundedness of the Hermite operator with complex time. Weissler's conjecture has important implications in several areas of mathematics including combinatorics, computer science, probability, isoperimetry, and approximation theory. The new techniques will be based on developing "two-point" inequalities. The second  direction of this research is to develop methods of harmonic analysis to find good estimates on the norms of various linear operators acting on a class of functions on the Hamming cube whose Fourier spectra belong to given prescribed sets. The basic examples include Bernstein-Markov type inequalities and their reverse forms for functions on the Hamming cube that live on the low and high frequencies respectively. The third direction is to understand the universality phenomena of the Gaussian measure. In particular, the goal is to investigate uniqueness of the functional Ehrhard inequality, which is the sharp analog of Brunn-Minkowski inequality for the Gaussian measure. The analysis will be based on Monge-Ampere type partial differential equations and semigroup methods. The fourth direction is to develop the duality between martingale inequalities related to sharp dyadic square function estimates and the problems of isoperimetric type; that is, gradient estimates for functions on the Hamming cube. Our methods will use heat envelopes, "four-point" inequalities, and "inf-sup" Legendre transform. The fifth direction aims to obtain sharp forms of the classical triangle inequalities in the Lp spaces using the theory of developable surfaces and minimal concave functions.

abstractText:
CAREER: Mechanism of Cytochrome P450 Alkene Biosynthesis

With this CAREER award, the Chemistry of Life Processes in the Chemistry Division of NSF is funding Dr. Thomas Makris from the University of South Carolina to study the mechanism of OleT, a recently discovered enzyme that is involved in the synthesis of hydrocarbons.  The biocatalytic production of hydrocarbons provides a potential route to sustainably produce fuels that are compatible within the existing energy infrastructure.  The atypical reaction catalyzed by OleT consumes hydrogen peroxide, a toxic reactive oxygen species, and transforms biologically abundant fatty acids into alkenes without any additional input of energy.  The goal of this research is to understand both the chemistry of this reaction, and the molecular details which promote it.  Additional broader impacts of this research are in its active involvement of undergraduate and high school students, and the community at large, in an ongoing protein engineering initiative that introduces this hydrocarbon producing capacity into a related enzyme.  The award also supports research for undergraduates from the home institution, and abroad, through a collaborative exchange with a liberal arts college for women, and provides the first research opportunities to high-school students from underrepresented minorities.

The cytochromes P450 are a ubiquitously expressed superfamily of thiolate-ligated heme enzymes that catalyze a diverse set of physiologically important chemical reactions.  Cytochrome P450 enzymes typically insert oxygen atoms into organic substrates using a ferryl intermediate known as Compound I.  OleT forms Compound I, but instead catalyzes a fundamentally different reaction that does not involve oxygen insertion.  The origins for this unusual metal-oxo reprogramming are being probed by biochemical, kinetics, spectroscopic and structural methods.  These methodologies evaluate the individual contributions of electronic structure, secondary coordination sphere, and substrate positioning on promoting the carbon-carbon scission reaction.  Dr. Makris has devised an innovative educational plan, termed Fats to Fuels, that is well integrated into the proposed studies of OleT.  In this plan, undergraduate students and the local community are engaged in learning how fats can be converted to hydrocarbon fuel sources. This research has the potential to impact society with respect to developing new hydrocarbon sources as alternatives to fossil fuels.

projectOutComesReport:
PROJECT OUTCOMES REPORT

CAREER: Mechanism of Cytochrome P450 Alkene Biosynthesis (CHE1555066) 

 

Intellectual Merit

This NSF grant aimed to understand the mechanism of a newly discovered enzyme termed OleT. At the inception of this grant, it was recognized that OleT, a member of the cytochrome P450 (CYP) superfamily, was involved in the decarboxylation of fatty acid substrates using hydrogen peroxide as a terminal product. The major product of the reaction, a terminal alkene one carbon shorter than the parent substrate, serves as an advanced “drop-in” biofuel as well as a commodity chemical. From a mechanistic perspective, OleT differs from other CYPs which typically insert oxygen into substrates in what is termed a monooxygenation reaction. Our work on this grant has focused on understanding how OleT differs from other CYPs in its ability to decarboxylate fatty acids (i.e. perform carbon-carbon cleavage rather than monooxygenation. Through identification of the one carbon coproduct (carbon dioxide, CO2) and the use of rapid kinetics measurements, we showed that C-C scission proceeded via a very similar heme-iron intermediate (an Fe4+-OH species) as that shown for monooxygenation and through a very similar process (hydrogen atom transfer). However, the next steps profoundly differ in that OleT does not perform oxygen rebound. Thus, a key mechanistic question that arose from these early studies was the role of the protein active-site  in promoting alkene formation. The role of the protein and substrate structure on steering OleT towards monooxygenation was probed in a variety of ways. Using substrate analogs, we established that substrate-type (e.g. fatty acid chain length) was critical for reinforcing this chemistry. This interplay was further established through alteration of the protein structure, as introduced alterations at sites quite distant from the site of chemistry radically altered the chemical outcome. Finally, structure/function correlations were further established through the study of various orthologs of OleT (i.e. proteins of similar sequence/structure, but with varying propensities for C-C cleavage versus monooxygenation). Taken together, the studies of OleT have shown how heme-iron enzymes can catalyze very different reactions through (a) controlling the reactivity of specific oxidizing species, and (b) binding substrates in a defined manner. These outcomes have significant relevance both for leveraging OleT for hydrocarbon synthesis and for the development of synthetic processes that aim to mimic its biochemistry.

 

Broader Impacts

The broader impacts of this grant have been in the training of STEM students at various levels of their educations (from high-school to (post)graduate) in an ongoing protein engineering project, using OleT as a scaffold for study. Tangible outcomes have included the active involvement of over 20 undergraduates and 3 high school students that received their first opportunities in inquiry-based research in the laboratory. Training within the laboratory has involved a diverse group of students and a significant number of historical minorities in the STEM workforce. At the graduate level, six students that received partial support from this project successfully defended their PhD dissertations and have gone on to successful careers in various sectors of government, industry, and academia.  One additional student from the NSF funded Interdisciplinary Biochemistry Master’s program (IBMP) received a master’s degree and transitioned to a career in biotechnology. In addition to training students within the laboratory, the project has also involved a broader community of trainees. An undergraduate biochemistry laboratory course was completely redeveloped using OleT as a scaffold of study. Students were introduced to concepts in (a) protein structure and design, (b) heterologous protein overproduction and purification, and (c) protein characterization. The laboratory established an inquiry-based approach to develop variants of OleT that improved/impaired activity. Results were then rationalized based on anticipated structural changes of the protein through analysis of crystallographic data.

abstractText:
How much can quantum algorithms outperform classical algorithms? This open question has been recently formulated as a mathematical problem that  has challenged the mathematical community but has yet to be solved. The question is related to another one: what is the most "efficient" way to encode and transmit given information? For example, a) one can try to  minimize the number of symbols used in encoding the information, or b) one can maintain "certain structures" (say by repeating some "pattern") in encoded messages in order to avoid loss of information, provided that a couple of errors can be made during its transmission. The goal of this project is to investigate what the best way is to approximate given information or a given signal using only zeros and ones. The principal investigator will involve undergraduate and graduate students in research projects described in the proposal. The PI will organize a yearly summer school in analysis and probability for graduate students. This will be a good opportunity for PhD students to participate in research discussions with leading experts and to learn about emerging areas in mathematics. 

The question of quantum algorithms described above can be formulated as an explicit Fourier–analytic question on the boolean cube. On a technical level the proposal focuses on hypercontractivity, i.e., boundedness of a semigroup between normed spaces, its holomorphic extensions to complex domains, applications in moment comparison estimates, Markov—Bernstein type inequalities (for polynomials living on low and high frequencies), discrete approximation theory, and complexity of classical and quantum algorithms. One of the important examples  involves the  Hamming cube, equipped with a product  measure. This project focuses on dimension independent estimates and proposes a program, a series of fundamental questions together with steps towards the resolution of these questions (heat flow arguments, martingale techniques, conformal maps,  and probabilistic arguments), necessary for advancing and developing Fourier analysis on the Boolean cube.

abstractText:
Symmetries play a fundamental role across the spectrum of mathematical sciences, especially as a unifying principle in physics. Classically symmetries of a physical system are described by algebraic objects known as groups, which act on the observables of the system. In quantum systems, however, the observables are described by noncommutative operator algebras (C* and von Neumann algebras). In this setting a new kind of symmetry emerges. The algebraic objects that naturally arise are called tensor categories, and have proved to be very successful at describing symmetries of low dimensional quantum field theories, topological phases of matter, and quantum statistical mechanics. The goal of this project is to apply the theory of tensor categories to understand the relationship between noncommutative operator algebras, as well as exploring the role of tensor categories in low dimensional quantum systems.

This project focuses on three main problems. The first is to use tensor categories to classify and construct discrete inclusions of von Neumann algebras building on recent progress in this area, furthering the work of the PI with David Penneys and with Shamindra K. Ghosh. The second is the study of Alain Connes' chi invariant for finite von Neumann algebras from the point of view of braided tensor categories. We propose a generalization of this invariant using non-invertible bimodules, along with new methods of computation of this invariant that will allow us to distinguish previously indistinguishable classes of von Neumann algebras. Finally, we investigate the algebraic process of gauging braided tensor categories, which described the interaction between quantum and classical symmetry in topological phases of condensed matter systems. This is an important construction from the physical point of view, but mathematically difficult to understand. The primary problem for this project is to establish the  existence of gauged categories in physically relevant situations such as permutation symmetry, generalizing the results of the PI with Terry Gannon.

projectOutComesReport:
Tensor categories are algebraic objects that capture a generalized notion of symmetry in the context of operator algebras, and play an important role in the study of topological defects of quantum spin systems. In this project, the PI developed a theory of tensor categorical symmetry of operator algebras from several perspectives and applied these paradigms to solve a handful of classification problems.

In joint work with Chen and Penneys, the PI introduced a new invariant of operator algebras called the categorical Chi invariant, and used it to distinguish a large class of non-commutative probability spaces called II1 factors, which arise naturally from the theory of subfactors, but were previously indistinguishable. This work uncovered a surprising connection between the theory of II1 factors and algebraic quantum field theory.

In joint work with Chen and Hernandez Palomares, the PI developed a theory of actions of tensor categories on C*-algebras, and introduced a new topological invariant for actions which was utilized to give a complete classification of approximately finite-dimensional quantum symmetries. This theorem is a new result even for the case of ``classical" group symmetries.

Other significant outcomes that were obtained by the PI include applications of higher categorical algebra to the study of topological domain walls between topological phases of matter, understanding symmetry enriched invariants of low-dimensional quantum field theories from a higher categorical perspective, and the construction of quantum symmetries on classical topological spaces. In addition, the PI is mentoring 6 PhD projects directly emerging from the results of this project.

abstractText:
Intelligent tutors are computer systems that use technologies such as artificial intelligence to provide learners with personalized instruction and feedback.  They have been shown to be highly effective at improving students' learning, largely because of their ability to provide students with individualized, adaptive support as they learn. This project aims to advance the technology for building intelligent tutors.  To do so, it will develop a framework for building intelligent tutors that makes it easier to create personalized learning experiences that adapt to individual learners.  The resulting intelligent tutoring system will use data to determine what actions the system should take, when the system should act, and explain why these actions should lead to improved learning.  This new intelligent tutoring system has the potential to transform STEM learning environments by providing accessible, low-cost, individualized instruction for complex STEM topics. 

This project will develop a generalizable data-driven framework to induce a wide range of instructional interventions and robust, yet flexible pedagogical decision-making policies across three STEM fields (logic, probability, and programming) and types of intervention (worked examples, buggy examples, and Parsons problems).  The system will be designed to allow use of the intelligent tutor in a wide range of STEM-related domains.  The system will use advanced machine learning and data mining techniques to generate instructional interventions, mixed-initiative pedagogical policies, and human-in-the-loop explanations.  This research will advance knowledge about data-driven generation of mixed-initiative decision making that balances a student’s sense of agency with their need for effective instructional interventions at critical decision points.  The efficacy of the resulting system will be evaluated via a series of empirical studies comparing the new interventions with existing tutoring systems to determine the impact on learning outcomes, agency, personalization, and effective interactions.  This project is supported by the NSF Improving Undergraduate STEM Education Program: Education and Human Resources.   The IUSE: EHR program supports research and development projects to improve the effectiveness of STEM education for all students. This project is in the Engaged Student Learning track, through which the program supports the creation, exploration, and implementation of promising practices and tools.

abstractText:
Predictive computational models play a central role not only in engineering and the sciences, but also in society at large. This project addresses fundamental issues common to virtually all computational models. If a model is too simple, the underlying phenomenon will not be faithfully described; if a model is too complex, its predictive power will be minimal. There is, somewhere, a happy middle; this project is about how to find the right balance in terms of model complexity. How complex should a computational model be to be useful? Both the mathematical community and domain scientists have long been worried about the lower bound – the minimum complexity. Models have be faithful to the underlying biology, chemistry or physics but how much of the science should one include? Quantum and relativistic effects can safely be ignored on many problems but what should be included and what can be left out to describe complex chemical reactions or physiological models? This project is about finding the lowest complexity sufficient for the tasks at hand. Models of complex systems, however, present features that render the task of making prediction with quantified uncertainties challenging. Such features include high-dimensional uncertain input parameters, time and/or space dependent quantities of interest, inherent stochasticity, as well as computational expense of simulating complex models. Research in this project will bring about key advances in modeling under uncertainty by developing mathematical techniques and computational methods to address such challenges in models of complex systems. The overarching goal is to develop methods that allow domain scientists to simplify their models so as to facilitate forward uncertainty quantification and parameter estimation at reasonable costs. Students will be trained and mentored in the interdisciplinary aspects of this project. In addition, his project involves the development of new course material that reflects and addresses challenges in present-day scientific computing.

The research in this project makes important contributions to computational modeling under uncertainty by developing mathematical theory and algorithms for (i) multiscale sensitivity analysis of stochastic compartment models, (ii) derivative- and variance-based sensitivity analysis methods for time-dependent stochastic systems, (iii) model complexity reduction in compartment models, and (iv) goal oriented multilevel dimension reduction for fast parameter estimation. The algorithms will be applied to models from biochemistry and physiology. A family of complex models of neurovascular coupling will be analyzed with the methods to be developed during the project, including dimension reduction, model complexity reduction and parameter estimation based on existing murine data. The model complexity reduction framework can be used in a broad range of models, where modelers can benefit from removing certain model components. Overall, by enabling dimension reduction in broad classes of models, the project bridges gaps in the processes of modeling, prediction under uncertainty, and parameter estimation: models with most essential components will be discovered and computational budget can be focused on quantifying uncertainty in only those model parameters that are most important to model output.

projectOutComesReport:
Mathematical models are are essential to understanding complex systems arising from engineering and science applications. Examples include models describing flow of contaminants, spread of wildfire, spread of infectious diseases, or biochemical reactions such as enzyme kinetics. Such models often have a large number of parameters that are not known exactly and are subject to uncertainty. To obtain reliable predictions, it is necessary to account for such uncertainties. This requires deploying tools from the field of uncertainty quantification, which provides mathematical, statistical, and computational tools for obtaining predictions with quantified uncertainties. A key aspect of uncertainty quantification is global sensitivity analysis (GSA). This helps understand the extent to which the different uncertain model parameters contribute to the uncertainty in the predictions. As such, GSA helps provide insight into the properties of the model, identify parameters that are most influential to model variability, and guide design of experiments. GSA also helps reducing the dimensionality of uncertain parameter vector, which in turn helps accelerate computational modeling and prediction under uncertainty.

However, GSA for models governing complex system is challenging. This is due in part to high cost of simulating such models as well as presence of a large number of uncertain parameters.  This results of this project provided several key advances in the field of sensitivity analysis and uncertainty quantification. These include novel approaches for approximating complex input-output relations as well as new GSA tools tailored to tasks such as parameter estimation, estimation of rare event probabilities, and model simplification.


In addition to research results, the funding from this grant was instrumental in training two PhD students who were supported by this project at different times. The graduate students supported by this grant were able to significantly improve their technical skills as well as professional skills such as effective written and verbal communication. The PIs also developed and presented tutorials and seminar talks on sensitivity analysis and uncertainty quantification. These outreach activities were designed to broaden the impact of the results from this project and to help train the next generation of researchers and practitioners in the field of computational modeling under uncertainty.

abstractText:
Large-scale anomalous emissions of greenhouse gases and air pollution pose threats to human health in the vicinity of the emissions, compromise state emissions targets, and threaten energy security.  Two recent, high-profile natural gas blowouts underscore the need for early detection and intervention. Several new and forthcoming satellites have the specific purpose of detecting and monitoring greenhouse gas emissions, and recent studies have demonstrated the potential of detecting such events using satellite data. However, there are enormous computational challenges in quantifying these emission anomalies or super-emitters due to the massive amounts of satellite data to be processed and the fine-scale resolution at which reconstructions are needed for threat detection. This project aims to tackle these challenges by developing improved computational methods for use in detection of atmospheric emissions. The project supports one graduate per year at each of the three universities.

The project aims to address fundamental issues in the development of computationally efficient solvers for inverse problems, and to push the traditional boundaries of threat detection via satellites by enabling researchers to detect and monitor anomalous atmospheric emissions quickly, accurately, and with quantifiable uncertainty. The main thrusts of this project are (i) efficient incorporation of prior information and parameter selection, (ii) improved spatio-temporal inverse modeling with multiple stochastic components and cost-cutting inexact and sampling approaches to handle expensive adjoint models, and (iii) evaluations, testing, and integration of the developed methods via case studies with synthetic satellite data. The aim of this project is to help identify potential immediate threats (e.g., oil and gas blowouts) using satellites, which have significant broader impacts not only in disaster response and recovery but also in minimizing the long-term environmental risks.

projectOutComesReport:
In recent years, high-profile anomalies or super-emitters have played an increasing role in the national conversation about greenhouse gas (GHG) and air pollution emissions because of the threats they pose to energy security (i.e., the availability of natural resources for energy consumption), public health, and safety. These leaks not only threaten state GHG emissions targets but also threaten the reliability and efficiency of the energy supply chain, occupational safety at gas facilities, human health in the vicinity of emissions, and contribute to air pollution exceedances.

 

In this project, we developed computational methods and tools to enable fast and accurate atmospheric inverse modeling for threat detection.  We advanced computational techniques for detecting and monitoring facilities that have abnormally large, disproportionate atmospheric emissions, so-called “super-emitters”; we developed robust algorithms, with data-informed automatic parameter selection, that can incorporate complex priors and handle very large geospatial datasets, and we established a robust evaluation and feedback procedure for working with new remote sensing satellite data to detect threats due to anomalous emissions.

 

The award has resulted in 7 peer-reviewed publications, in esteemed journals such as the SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing, Geoscientfic Model Development, SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications, and Advances in Computational Mathematics. The research developments have been broadly disseminated in the scientific community. In addition to over 30 invited talks and colloquia given by the PIs Chung, Miller, and Saibaba, including multiple prestigious plenary talks. Students and postdocs gave numerous contributed talks at national and international conferences during this award.  The project also supported the development and dissemination of open-source code available on GitHub, for wide impact.

abstractText:
In this collaborative project, co-funded by the Chemical Structure, Dynamics & Mechanisms B and the Chemical Structure, Dynamics & Mechanisms A programs of the Chemistry Division, Professor Lin X. Chen of the Department of Chemistry at Northwestern University and Professor Felix N. Castellano from the Department of Chemistry at North Carolina State University lead a project to understand the effects of coherent electronic motions in energy and electron transfer in distinct classes of multi-chromophoric synthetic platforms.  The knowledge obtained through the proposed studies will greatly enhance the ability to rationally design chemical materials/devices for catalysis, optoelectronics, and energy sustainability.  The proposed research engages University graduate students to use advanced laser spectroscopy for characterization, incorporates state-of-the-art computational chemistry for quantum mechanical and molecular dynamics modeling, and utilizes advanced chemistry laboratory facilities for molecular syntheses and structural characterization, engendering them with expansive training necessary for the development of multidisciplinary scientific expertise.   The proposed research/education activities are integrated with numerous K-12 public outreach activities at both universities, including Photonics Day at North Carolina State University and NU Bond at Northwestern University.   

Specifically, they will employ newly developed two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy in their studies with very high time resolution of approximately 6 femtoseconds. The rationally designed molecules are engineered to tune electronic coupling in their excited states, which are either responsible for or can be correlated to electronic coherence originating from in-phase motions of electrons induced by photoexcitation. The measured coherences will be correlated with the observation of photoinduced intramolecular energy and/or electron transfer chemistry and rationalized using continuously developing theory to assess the role of electronic and/or vibronic coherence in these fundamental primary processes related to light activation. Two types of molecular designs are targeted for these investigations: (1) Pt(II) dimers bridged by hydroxypyridines featuring metal-metal-to-ligand charge transfer excited states where a metal-metal bond is transiently formed following light excitation; and (2) Pt(II) dimers whose terminal cyclometalating ligands are decorated with bay-substituted naphthalenediimide based energy and/or electron acceptors.  The proposed project seeks to glean new insight into excited state chemistry and how this knowledge can be leveraged to control reactivity in condensed phases, molecular photonics, and photocatalysis.

projectOutComesReport:
The overarching theme of this collaborative project between the Castellano (North Carolina State University) and Chen (Northwestern University) laboratories was to investigate systematic structural control over light-triggered metal-metal bond-forming processes in precisely controlled molecular architectures and their subsequent relaxation processes resulting in the breaking of this same metal-metal bond. This research ultimately seeks an understanding of intrinsic electronic couplings between two metal centers in transition metal-containing molecules and their influence on photochemical reactivity. Specifically, we designed multiple series of transition metal-based dimers where a metal-metal bond is formed following visible light excitation between two Pt(II) metal centers held together in close spatial proximity. These molecules exhibit distance-dependent light absorption, electrochemical, and photophysical behavior, structurally varied applying rational chemical synthesis approaches resulting in the modulation of the metal-metal distances and relative geometries through the structural design of the ligand frameworks. The work at NC State focused on the design, synthesis, and structural characterization of the molecules at the heart of the study while the work at Northwestern applied sophisticated ultrafast spectroscopies revealing the excited state evolution of these molecules as a function of time. The latter used ultrashort excitation laser pulses as short as 7 femtoseconds to accomplish cutting-edge ultrafast optical transient absorption and two-dimensional spectroscopy on these molecules for the first time. The most impactful results from these investigations were recently reported in the scientific journal Nature in 2023, which revealed the interplay between the dynamics of electron spin and the vibrational dynamics of the nuclei in molecules on superfast time scales, which is termed the spin-vibronic effect. Electron spin and vibrational motion cannot be treated independently as they mix and affect electronic dynamics in a complex manner, moving beyond the assumptions of the Born-Oppenheimer approximation wherein the motion of nuclei and electrons in a molecule are independent of each other and can be treated separately. The breakdown of this assumption was a consequence of performing experiments on the 7 femtosecond timescale, revealing the close relationship between the dynamics of nuclei and electrons in the Pt(II) chromophores at the heart of this investigation. This spin-vibronic effect in these molecules altered their energy landscape, increasing the probability and rate of intersystem crossing while revealing intermediate electronic states that were integral to the operation of the spin-vibronic effect. Our discovery could influence the design of molecules useful for solar energy conversion, energy production, quantum information science, and beyond.

Our research engaged graduate students and postdoctoral associates to use advanced laser spectroscopy for characterization, incorporated state-of-the-art computational chemistry for quantum mechanical and molecular dynamics modeling, and utilized advanced chemistry laboratory facilities for molecular synthesis, providing them with an expansive training ground for developing multidisciplinary expertise. Such training is essential for the next generation STEM workforce to explore the frontiers of the chemical sciences and ensure US global competitiveness at the frontiers of scientific knowledge. The diverse and interdisciplinary project has primarily supported a female doctoral graduate researcher over the duration of the award and one undergraduate student supported during the summer months at North Carolina State University. The NC State and Northwestern collaborators have extensively collaborated in the pursuit of this project, resulting in several co-authored peer-reviewed manuscripts and presentations at numerous professional scientific meetings throughout the duration of the award period.

abstractText:
Web applications have become a major platform to deliver various services to the general public, largely due to the increasing popularity of cloud services for hosting web applications and handheld devices for accessing web applications. Poor-quality web applications can lead to significant problems, including user dissatisfaction and financial losses. A key challenge imposed by web applications is due to their request-driven nature; they expose services to users and serve requests with application-defined request-handler methods. Under this request-driven paradigm, inter-request control and data dependencies exist although each request is served independently. However, tracking these dependencies across requests is challenging because of the diversity and complexity of languages and frameworks for implementing web applications. Existing techniques targeting web applications lack any inter-request analysis capability, and they may miss performance-optimization opportunities and security issues that can only be exposed in the inter-request context.

This project promotes inter-request analysis to handle the problems just cited. To build a solid foundation for inter-request analysis, this project designs and develops techniques that can effectively and efficiently capture and express control and data dependencies across requests. The proposed techniques combine statistical mining approaches with a hybrid of static and dynamic analyses. The generated workflow and dataflow models provide necessary inter-request knowledge for various analyses to extend the scope. With the inter-request workflow- and dataflow-modeling framework, this project explores performance optimization and workflow monitoring to improve the quality of web applications regarding performance, correctness, and security. From the success of previous research on inter-procedural and inter-thread analyses for handling the abstraction of procedures and threads, the concept of inter-request analysis can greatly benefit web applications and other request-driven applications through both technique development and student education.
