projectOutComesReport:
Intellectual Merit: The project introduced the concept of inter-request analysis, developing innovative techniques to effectively capture and express control and data dependencies across web application requests. These techniques combined statistical mining with hybrid static and dynamic analyses to generate comprehensive workflow and dataflow models. These models enable deeper insights into performance optimization and workflow monitoring, significantly enhancing the quality of web applications in terms of performance, correctness, and security.

 

With our modeling framework, we were able to identify performance optimization opportunities and suggest possible optimization strategies. To enrich the types of performance inefficiencies that can be detected and optimized, we conducted an extensive study of real-world performance bugs. By analyzing these bugs, we learned common patterns and developed corresponding fixing strategies. Our research focused on understanding how these inefficiencies occur and devising methods to mitigate them. On the concurrency front, we developed an approach to model happens-before relationships between web application requests. This approach helps in identifying races, which occur when multiple requests interfere with each other in unintended ways. Using this model, we created a dynamic race detection tool capable of detecting server-side races with a low false positive rate. This tool is crucial for maintaining the integrity and performance of web applications. Further studies on server-side races and deadlocks in web applications revealed unique characteristics and complexities, which were previously unexplored. These findings have provided a deeper understanding of how web applications operate under concurrent request conditions and have led to new techniques for detecting and resolving these issues.

 

Additionally, the project investigated request races that break the idempotency of request handlers, which ensure that repeated requests do not cause unintended side effects. We provided guidance to developers on building idempotent request handlers effectively and developed static analysis techniques to identify potential request races. Our findings help programmers understand the relationship between request races and idempotency, offering essential guidance on building reliable web applications.

 

We also examined exception-handling bugs in web applications, categorizing them into missing handling bugs and improper handling bugs. Our results indicate that missing handling bugs are more common and should be the focus of future research. The detailed characterization from our study will guide the design of tools to detect and fix these bugs, further improving the reliability of web applications.

 

Broader Impacts: The outcomes of this project have far-reaching impacts beyond the immediate scope of web application development. By improving the performance and reliability of web applications, the techniques developed can benefit a wide array of disciplines that rely on web-based services. This includes not only technology sectors but also any field that utilizes web applications to deliver services to the public, such as healthcare, education, and government services.

 

The project also contributed significantly to human resource development by training PhD students in various aspects of web application development. They gained experience in bug characterization, tool implementation, experimental evaluation, and result interpretation. This comprehensive training equipped them with valuable skills and knowledge, advancing their academic and professional careers and preparing them to contribute effectively to the tech industry and academia.

 

Overall, the project's advancements in web application analysis and optimization promise to enhance the user experience and operational efficiency of web services. By ensuring more reliable and performant web applications, this research benefits society at large. Users can enjoy smoother, faster, and more secure web experiences, which is increasingly important in our digital age where so much of our daily lives depend on web applications. This project not only advances the state of web application technology but also provides crucial insights and tools that can be used by developers worldwide to build better, more efficient web applications.

abstractText:
Each of the nearly 20 million students that attended American colleges and universities in Fall 2019 had his or her education disrupted due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Colleges and universities responded quickly and dynamically to help mitigate disease spread while continuing to deliver a high-quality learning experience. Mitigation strategies involved rapid transitions to online learning, closure of on-campus housing with little to no notice, and drastic changes to student and university life over several weeks. The disruption has drastically changed our communities, and these changes may be particularly challenging for our most vulnerable students, including ones with housing and hunger insecurity or behavioral health issues. This RAPID project, Matriculation and Well-Being Under Emergent Events (MWEE), will utilize time-sensitive data associated with the COVID-19 pandemic to study student well-being. MWEE will focus on engineering students in undergraduate programs where a component of course success is often hands-on labs and teamwork. MWEE will harness data from five campuses, engage communities and encourage the development of processes and actions to address this global challenge. The institutions include a private university, a public university, and three land-grant universities, one of which is a historically black college and university (HBCU). Geographic regions include the South, Midwest and Pacific Northwest. 

A better understanding of critical factors that influence the success of vulnerable students can provide insight for developing effective interventions for reducing college attrition associated with COVID-19. The knowledge can also potentially inform university decisions regarding response to other emergent events. MWEE aims to (i) collect and synthesize structured and unstructured data from multiple sources that relate to the health and behavior of students and (ii) utilize machine learning and optimization techniques to learn from the data to identify best practices, identify students at risk, and inform potential policies and interventions. The MWEE methodology will create a new convergent scientific paradigm to understand, assess, and measure individual and community well-being and resilience during complex and novel situations such as the COVID-19 pandemic. It is expected that universities will be able to layer the results with data from their campuses to predict retention and graduation rates given emergent events including COVID-19.

program: COVID-19 Research, RAPID
projectOutComesReport:
The COVID-19 pandemic has challenged our college and universities to respond quickly and dynamically to help mitigate disease spread. This has involved rapid transitions to online learning, closure of on-campus housing with little to no notice, and drastic changes to student and university life. This has radically  changed our communities in ways that may be particularly challenging for students with food and housing insecurity or behavioral health issues. The Matriculation and Well-Being Under Emergent Events (MWEE) project has studied the impact of COVID-19 university policies adopted to control disease spread on college students. It specifically considers a broad range of issues faced in emerging adulthood that contribute to disparities in well-being. In particular, MWEE collected ephemeral data associated with the COVID-19 pandemic to study its impact on student well-being.

For the nearly 20 million emerging adults (i.e., ages 18-29) in the US, college offers the opportunity to positively or negatively impact their life trajectories. Emerging adulthood is a critical developmental stage where people identify and commit to roles, relationships, and responsibilities of adulthood. Stressors such as hunger, homelessness, and behavioral health issues negatively impact belonging, graduation, employment, and financial stability. College students consistently seek support for anxiety, depression, and suicidality, with 56% and 45% facing housing and food insecurity, respectively. These stressors take a toll on student health, wealth and education outcomes well past the time a student drops out or graduates. The COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated this stress, further exposing the disparities in college student well-being, and challenging colleges and universities to innovate.

This research has collected heterogeneous structured and unstructured longitudinal data including weekly student report of well-being over the course of the 2020-2021 and 2021-2022 academic years, student geolocation data, student performance data, and institutional policy information to map the psychological well-being dimensions to quantifiable metrics for assessing well-being dynamically and enable intelligent intervention. Well-being is multi-dimensional and has complex interactions across subjective and objective measures including mental, social, activities and functioning, physical, spiritual, emotional, intellectual, psychological, occupational, environmental and personal circumstance. The measurement and modeling of social and psychological constructs (e.g., identity, values, behavioral intention, etc.) driving health behavior and the processing of information about health is an active and open area of research: particularly with respect to efforts to validly and reliably measure well-being and other related constructs. It is necessary to create an engineered representation of social and behavioral responses to stimuli and interventions. Our collaborative grant, MWEE, has initiated this process. Existing studies have focused on shorter follow-up periods with a focus on predicting a change in well-being. These studies have not sought to model the evolution of student well-being. We extend this research to model the evolution of student well-being over the course of an academic semester. In addition, we have used the student performance data to model student academic well-being over the course of an academic program with the goal of understanding engineering student dropout. This longitudinal approach that makes predictions at key milestones through a student’s matriculation contributes to both the understanding of student well-being and methodologically to modeling the evolution of student performance.

As college students continue to struggle with the aftereffects of the COVID-19 pandemic including significant mental health challenges associated with adjusting to the trauma of the last several years, it is even more important to be able to use ephemeral data from this period to understand its impact on student well-being. Better understanding of key factors which influence the success of vulnerable students can provide insight for developing effective interventions for reducing college attrition associated with COVID-19 and potentially inform university decisions regarding response to extreme events such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Through this project, we identified differences in students’ self-report of anxiety and other well-being factors as a function of student movement during the night. The university and survey data can be mapped to psychological theory regarding well-being and can be used to estimate enrollment for the following year and to predict the “risk of a student dropping out” and the likelihood of graduation. For this project, we partnered with university Enrollment Management and Services management to better understand student dropout. Our analysis of the student performance data has been shared with the university leadership and has begun to inform how they think about student dropout and factors that may be used to mitigate it. This project has developed a framework for assessing student well-being over time and understanding these and other factors impact student performance in order to design effective early intervention strategies.

abstractText:
Emerging Non-Volatile Memories (NVMs) promise convergence of memory and storage into a single system that is both fast and persistent. Existing security functions for storage systems were designed for slower storage devices, which create a performance bottleneck for faster NVMs.  This research will investigate high performance security solutions for NVM based storage systems. 
 
The first research thrust will focus on encrypting data for emerging NVMs. The second thrust investigates implementation of auditing mechanisms for NVM based storage systems.
 
The proposed project will train graduate and undergraduate students on architecting secure systems. The results from this research will inform several undergraduate and graduate courses. Students from underrepresented groups will be encouraged to participate in this project. The results will be published in reputed conferences and journals. 

The project data and results will be published and maintained in both private and public repositories. The project will use Github site: https://github.com/sacagroup/sacagroup.github.io. All project data, codes and results will be maintained for at least 5 years after the end of the project.

projectOutComesReport:
Intellectual Merits: 

The project identified challenges for enabling certain features of emerging persistent memories while supporting filesystem encryption and auditing. Accordingly, novel mechanisms to bridge such a gap were devised and evaluated. The techniques include hardware/software co-designs to address the identified challenges, and performance optimizations to make such solutions more practical. Additionally, the project explored challenges to realize such solutions and general persistent security in upcoming memory interfaces and platform support. The project resulted major publications in top-tier conferences and journals in the field of computer architecture disseminating the proposed designs and identified challenges. 

 

Broader Impact: 

The outcomes of this project were disseminated widely in academic conferences/journals, YouTube presentations, talks at major semiconductor companies and other academic institutions, and the results of this project were incorporated in a teaching material part of special topics courses offered at the PI's institution. Finally, the project trained students on cutting edge technologies, how to model it, security challenges arise upon using such technologies, and how to do pathfinding research to identify mitigations and solutions.  

 

Summary:

In summary, the project led to innovations of how we can enable efficient usage of persistent memories in computing systems while preserving the conventional security required for filesystems. Although high-overheads were initially observed, our investigation revealed that an efficient hardware/software co-design can lead to practical and low-overhead solutions when architected to exploit metadata locality and leverage certain secure memory optimizations.

abstractText:
General audience abstract

This project will explore nearly perfect fluid flow in a “designer” quantum system, comprising a unique ultracold gas of atoms, contained in a box made entirely of laser light. The atoms used in these tabletop experiments feature experimentally adjustable attraction or repulsion, from very weak to very strong, enabling measurements that impact theories in intellectual disciplines well outside of atomic physics. The contained atoms model new materials, such as super-high temperature superconductors that operate far above room temperature, which will one day enable energy-saving power lines and magnetically levitated trains. Students and post-doctoral associates will design new optical systems, new computer control and mechanical systems, and study electrodynamics and quantum mechanics, broadly training them for challenges arising in science and technology.

Technical audience abstract

The experiments will study the fluid dynamics of a Fermi gas of Li-6 atoms near a collisional (Feshbach) resonance, which enables magnetic control of atom-atom interactions. The ultracold Fermi gas is contained, perturbed, and imaged in a designer optical potential, which is generated using two digital micro-mirror arrays. By imaging the atom density profile as a function of time, the new experiments will measure the hydrodynamic linear response and transport properties as a function of temperature, interaction strength, and spin-imbalance. Imaging the trapped cloud in a 1D linearly varying potential will determine the equation of state. Designer optical potentials also will be used for in-situ imaging of shock waves as a function of interaction strength, density profile and temperature profile.

projectOutComesReport:
Optically-trapped, ultra-cold Fermi gases of spin 1/2-up and spin 1/2-down 6Li atoms model exotic systems in nature, including high temperature superconductors, neutron matter, and even the quark-gluon plasma, a state of matter at 2 trillion degrees, that existed microseconds after the Big Bang. In 6Li, a bias magnetic field tunes the gas to a collisional (Fano-Feshbach) resonance, where the dilute atomic cloud becomes a strongly interacting fluid, known as a unitary Fermi gas. For a unitary Fermi gas, the thermodynamic properties and hydrodynamic transport properties are universal functions of density and temperature, providing stringent parameter-free tests of state of the art predictions for strongly interacting many-body systems.

Early measurements of the shear viscosity of expanding unitary Fermi gas clouds with non-uniform density have made way for new measurements in optical box potentials, where the density is nearly uniform. The primary accomplishment of this program is the first demonstration of general methods for measuring hydrodynamic transport properties from the time-dependent free-decay of a spatially periodic density perturbation in an optical box potential.

The box comprises six sheets of repulsive (blue-detuned) light, projected from two digitally controlled micro-mirror devices (DMDs).  A third DMD projects a repulsive spatially periodic optical potential, creating a spatially periodic density perturbation along one direction in static equilibrium. Abruptly extinguishing the optical perturbation causes an oscillatory decay of the density perturbation.

The figure shows an initial sinusoidal density perturbation and subsequent evolution of the dominant Fourier component for a normal phase, unitary Fermi gas. The data is fit by a hydrodynamic model, which reveals an exponentially decaying, thermally diffusive mode (orange) and a decaying oscillating first sound mode (blue).  Together, the decay rates of these two modes determine both the thermal conductivity and the shear viscosity in a single experiment.

abstractText:
Digital data are being generated at increasingly overwhelming rates both economically and for the environment, with data storage material and energy usages close to reaching the physical limits of what current technologies can provide. For over two decades DNA has been considered with only limited enthusiasm as a potential next generation medium for data storage, despite holding pronounced advantages of high density, stability, and low energy requirements. This is because executing the core operations of a data storage system including write, access, read, and protect using DNA currently requires multiple complex steps carried out in succession. Furthermore, they often require specialized processing and purification in between each operational step. This leads to practical barriers in speed, cost, scalability, and reusability. The central hypothesis of this proposal is that an interdisciplinary collaboration can completely reimagine and reengineer these core operations to be continuous, highly practical, and economically viable through creative integration of knowledge and technologies from disparate disciplines. Specifically, molecular biology techniques from the Biological Sciences will be informed and designed by models and simulations derived from the discipline of Computer Science and Engineering, while these biological components will be physically controlled and interfaced with nanomaterials developed with expertise in Materials Science and Nanoscience. This hybrid information storage system engineered from DNA directly interfaced with novel nanofibrillar substrates, will leverage dynamic processing by biomolecular manipulations, and will unlock direct and rapid readout of information with semiconductor-based nanopore technology. Biomolecular-based computational modeling will inform all aspects of both the design of the system and its operation, from molecular to systems level scales. The interdisciplinary nature of this project will also provide strong opportunities to advance education and diversity in the Science-Technology-Engineering-Math (STEM) workforce through several avenues. This interdisciplinary research provides opportunities for undergraduate researchers to experience directly working with peers and PhD students from very different disciplines on common problems. Undergraduate course modules will be created that bridge synthetic biology, nanoscience, materials science, computer science and engineering that present applied interdisciplinary examples including DNA storage as case studies. Hands-on kits will also be developed to facilitate in-person and virtual activities administered through partnerships with organizations that reach and support underrepresented grade-school students in STEM. 

This project aims to transform DNA storage systems from batch to continuous architectures. Each Aim addresses a unit process (WRITE, ACCESS, READ, PROTECT). WRITE: Rapid, scalable, and cheap DNA synthesis will be engineered by a combination of tree algorithms and enzyme-driven DNA assembly. ACCESS: Continuous and reusable access of information and files will be achieved by immobilization of a DNA database on dendritic colloidal particles with easily accessible high surface areas. This novel scaffold allows a transcription-based file access system previously developed by the team to rapidly extract information in the form of transcribed RNA through simple laminar flow through the DNA database. READ: RNA generated by the ACCESS technology will be directly read by nanopore sequencing, and fundamental experimental and machine learning studies will be engaged to inform the encoding algorithms of DNA databases and to optimize real-time base-calling. PROTECT: The unique physical and thermodynamic attributes of DNA and of these first three hybrid unit processes will be exploited to encrypt and obfuscate information. While fundamental thermodynamic findings, computational models, and physical technologies generated in each aim have strong and specific benefits in mutually informing the other aims, these unit processes will further be integrated together by two ongoing explicit Umbrella Tasks. End-to-end microfluidic devices storing protected data will be engineered by integrating all unit processes, informed by systems-level modeling to identify unit processes that are the bottlenecks for speed, cost, robustness, and longevity. This work will also generate important fundamental knowledge and models that will be generalizable to other types of biomolecular-based information storage systems as well as applicable to problems in each distinct discipline regarding DNA assembly and interaction specificity, nanoparticle engineering, and nucleic acid sequencing.

projectOutComesReport:
Digital data are being generated at increasingly unsustainable rates, with data storage material and energy usages close to reaching the physical limits of current technologies can provide. DNA could be a potential next generation medium for data storage. It holds clears advantages of high density, stability, and low energy requirements. However, a major barrier to widespread adoption and application of DNA storage is that many of the unit processes developed to date are highly specialized, requiring multiple complex individual steps, and often suffer in speed, cost, scalability, and reusability. The central hypothesis of this project was that if unit processes can be engineered at the molecular scale in partnership with informative models and simulations, they can be made to be compatible with continuous processing and operation. The corollary is then that the development of continuous unit processes will increase the economically viable application space of DNA storage, from the maintenance and transportation of extreme-scale data down to small-scale disposable and portable single-use hard-drives, as well as reveal previously unanticipated benefits and uses of the technology. This project: created an end-to-end store and compute engine capable of storing data for thousands of years and computing chess and sudoku problems; advanced new technologies for encoding data into DNA and optimizing the architectures of DNA data storage systems; advanced technologies for synthesizing, moving, storing, and reading DNA; and revealed fundamentally new properties of DNA and exploited them for encryption purposes. This project also led to the training of multiple PhD, undergraduate, and high school students in areas of synthetic biology, computer systems engineering, bioinformatics, nanoscience, and materials engineering.

abstractText:
This work will provide a better understanding of the pathways of energy in the global ocean and the exchanges with the  atmosphere. These processes occur on different time and space scales and regulate Earth’s climate.  The ocean generally gains energy (heat) in the tropics from the sun, which is then transported poleward by major ocean currents along the western boundaries of ocean basins, such as the Gulf Stream, and eventually lost back to the atmosphere in the midlatitudes.  Recent research shows that oceanic turbulence in these midlatitude regions associated with strong current systems leads to a loss of energy to the atmosphere, not accounted for in traditional ocean circulation models.  This sink of energy to the atmosphere at these turbulent time and space scales modulates the ocean circulation in unforeseen ways that need further investigation.  This project will enhance our understanding of these processes and will develop parameterizations for their inclusion in general ocean circulation models leading to improving projections of Earth’s climate system. The study will combine remotely sensed data of sea surface height, surface temperature, and net heat flux collected over several decades with numerical simulations of coupled and uncoupled high-resolution Earth system models. The analysis will lead to better quantifying the rates and mechanisms of how energy is transferred from the ocean to the atmosphere and how this is associated with mesoscale eddies in the ocean. This proposal will support and help build the laboratory of an early career PI and the training of a PhD student. Public outreach lectures will be used to communicate the importance of the Gulf Stream in a changing climate.

This work will aid in a better understanding of the pathways of energy in the global ocean. High-resolution climate models persistently have high sea surface temperature variance, but surface EKE comparable to observations. This proposal will help shed light on why this discrepancy occurs. Work in the Kuroshio Extension using a regional coupled model shows that this sink accounts for more than 70% of the EPE that would be available for conversion to eddy kinetic energy (EKE). However, it is still an open question how the OME-A sink connects to a modulation of EKE globally. This study will use multiple decades of available remote-sensed surface observations and a suite of global high-resolution simulations in coupled and uncoupled configurations of the Community Earth System Model (CESM-H) to access energy conversion rates through a local and global analysis. A local analysis requires a decomposition of the eddy heat flux field into divergent and rotational fluxes. The principal investigator will use Helmholtz decomposition to solve the Poisson equation globally in order to extract the dynamically important divergent fluxes. The main objectives are to 1) determine how the OME-A feedback modulates the efficiency of baroclinic instability to convert potential to kinetic energy in CESM-H; and 2) examine the spatial and temporal scale dependence of the EPE sources and sinks in state-of-the-art observations and CESM-H. There will be particular focus on the northern hemisphere Western Boundary Currents and their correspondence with decadal climate modes such as the North Atlantic Oscillation and Pacific Decadal Oscillation. A new parameter will be defined that does not depend on absolute model energetics and will allow model evaluations in current and future High-Resolution Model Intercomparison Projects such as the international Laboratory for High-Resolution Earth System Prediction (iHESP). The proposed team will collaborate with participants in the climate process team (CPT) on ocean transport and eddy energy and will ultimately contribute to a framework for parameterization development of the OME-A EPE sink in coarse-resolution coupled climate models.

abstractText:
Influenced by air-sea heat exchange, rainfall, and evaporation, the buoyancy of the ocean’s uppermost layer can impact the overturning oceanic circulation. Winds above the ocean surface can generate currents and promote mixing. The combined effects of wind and buoyancy on the ocean are ultimately felt throughout the entire ocean. In response to the changing ocean conditions (especially, the sea surface temperature or SST), atmospheric circulations can arise to govern patterns of clouds and rain, which in turn impact the wind and buoyancy forcings on the ocean. To this end, mechanisms involving buoyancy and winds at the air-sea interface are critical in establishing the timescales, patterns, and amplitudes of many climate variations we observe and simulate in climate models. Yet, complete understanding of these mechanisms remains elusive due to sparse ocean observations and complicated dynamics. The research will decompose the relative effects of winds versus buoyancy forcing using climate model experiments, with emphasis on two features expected to substantially change in a future climate, namely the surface temperature and the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC).

In particular, many open questions remain about the importance of winds versus buoyancy forcing as pathways through which the atmosphere communicates intrinsic and externally forced variations to the ocean. Addressing these questions is made more difficult by a wide gap in the model hierarchy, between fully coupled models with a complete dynamical representation of both the ocean and atmosphere and models that represent the ocean as a motionless slab that is only thermally coupled to the atmosphere. This work will be implemented by closing said gap in the model hierarchy via leveraging a mechanically decoupled (MD) version of a climate model, which isolates variations in the ocean circulation that are driven solely by buoyancy from the wind-driven variability captured by fully coupled models. With the MD as an intermediate step between fully coupled and slab ocean models, a clearer mechanistic understanding of the drivers of climate variations is possible. These three model versions will be used together to identify the relative roles of buoyancy and wind variations in driving intrinsic SST variability, anthropogenic trends in surface temperature, and intrinsic and anthropogenically forced AMOC variations.

projectOutComesReport:
Variations in climate patterns occur on timescales from weeks to years to decades and beyond. These variations bring with them tangible changes to air and ocean temperatures and altered patterns of precipitation, thus affecting a wide variety of industries worldwide. The patterns that persist longest typically are tied to pronounced changes in ocean surface temperatures. A variety of natural processes drive these ocean surface temperature changes, namely air-sea heat exchange and wind blowing on the surface, which causes changes in ocean circulation and ocean heat transport. Another way to drive pronounced ocean temperature changes is through human-induced activities, namely the emissions of greenhouse gases and aerosols. The goals of this study were to 1) determine the relative importance of air-sea heat exchange versus wind driven changes to the ocean in setting ocean temperature variability, 2) discover whether wind driven ocean changes impact the rate and pattern of global warming, and 3) discover whether wind driven ocean changes impact the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, a large-scale piece of the ocean conveyor belt with wide reaching climate impacts. To achieve these goals, we designed climate model experiments that removed the effects of wind driven changes on the ocean and compared those with climate models that retained those effects. 

To address the first goal, we compared climate models with different ocean complexities. We found that overall, wind driven changes in the ocean increase the amplitude and persistence of ocean surface temperature variations. We also found that despite careful efforts, there are unintended consequences of using simplified ocean models, and these issues could cause one to misinterpret the reason for differences across models. We made specific recommendations to future users of these simulations on considerations for using the model set up to investigate drivers of climate variability. 

To address the second goal and determine how wind driven ocean changes impact the rate of global warming, we designed and ran a climate model ensemble in which the wind driven ocean circulation could not change even with the introduction of greenhouse gases and aerosols in the atmosphere. Notably, the ensemble without wind driven ocean changes warmed about 15% less than the model where winds could drive changes in the ocean circulation. We concluded that changes in the wind driven ocean circulation can amplify the rate of global warming, due to regionally dependent cloud feedbacks. In another study, we found that while both ensembles warmed, the ensemble with wind driven ocean changes had a larger range of warming possibilities than the ensemble without wind driven ocean changes. We concluded that wind driven ocean variability can delay the emergence of global warming trends, potentially masking the impacts of climate change in regions like the tropical oceans for up to two decades. 

For the third goal, we found that over the short-term, changes in the wind driven ocean do not impact the strength of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, but after several decades, weakened winds lead to less stirring in the high latitude ocean, setting off a process that causes rapid decline in the circulation strength. This weakening has a host of impacts, particularly on the climate over Greenland and western Europe. The weakening of the circulation also causes a local cooling effect in the North Atlantic subpolar ocean gyre. Further, we find that the spatial pattern and amplitude of this local cooling effect is highly dependent on how much greenhouse gas is emitted into the atmosphere, thus it is not a reliable “proxy” for strength of the circulation. 

This project provided a more complete view of the role of the ocean as the climate changes. Significant model development efforts were completed and shared with the broader community. This project produced model experiments that are now publicly available and have facilitated numerous published studies on the role of the wind driven ocean circulation in a changing climate beyond what was directly funded by the grant. Another important outcome of this project was the career and professional development of a postdoctoral scholar, who is now faculty at an R1 institution, and several graduate students, all of whom are successfully employed in their field of study.

abstractText:
NON-TECHNICAL DESCRIPTION: Ultrahard protective coatings are critical in applications ranging from microelectronics packaging to cutting tools needed for oil and gas extraction and high-speed machining. Performance improvement directly scales with the hardness enhancement of protective coatings. This proposal focuses on design and synthesis of ultrahard materials, striving to be harder than diamond — the hardest material known so far. By using a novel approach based upon rapid laser melting and quenching, it is possible to create diamond or new Q- phases of carbon which are significantly harder. Since this process can be performed at ambient temperatures and pressures, there is a significant reduction in energy usage and manufacturing of Q-carbon and diamond-related materials. This research is being integrated with the curriculum development and related educational activities, such as M.S. Nano program. The proposal addresses training of graduate and undergraduate students in collaboration with ORNL, Kopin Corporation and NC A&T to attract minority students into the graduate studies. 

TECHNICAL DETAILS: Diamond and Q-phase related materials are synthesized by nanosecond laser melting of carbon films and rapid quenching from the undercooled state. The degree of undercooling determines this direct conversion into diamond or Q-carbon or a mixture of the two. Modeling is carried out to understand laser-solid interactions and correlations between hardness and number density of atoms.  In this project, different Q-carbon and diamond mixtures are synthesized by controlling laser, film and sapphire substrate variables. These phases are characterized by using high-resolution electron microscopy, electron-energy-loss spectroscopy and Raman techniques, and direct correlations with enhanced hardness and toughness established.

Final  Outcomes for DMR- 2016256

DMR NSF Report Final  Outcomes: Designing Ultra-hard Coatings of Q-carbon and Diamond Related Materials

Principal Investigator: J. Narayan, John C. C. Fan Family Distinguished Chair in Materials Science, NAE member

Background and Introduction:

The hardness (H) of solids is directly related to shear modulus (µ) by H = αµ, where α is a constant with a value of about 0.2. The relation of hardness with Young’s modulus (E)  and bulk modulus in an isotropic solid (B) involves Poisson’s ratio (ν), which is the measure of transverse contraction to longitudinal extension.  The hardness (H) is related to E and B by H = α E [2(1 + ν)]-1 = 3α B (1 -2 ν) [2(1 + ν)]-1. The diamond has the highest hardness because of the highest bulk modulus, arising from covalently bonded strong σ bonds, and relatively low value of Poisson’s ratio of about 0.1.  We show that the bulk modulus is directly related to the number density of atoms. The highest hardness of diamond is directly related to the highest number density of atoms (1.77x1023 atoms cm-3). To exceed this value of hardness, we have increased the number density of covalently bonded atoms in the new lattice.

It is interesting to note that despite the highest number density of atoms, the diamond cubic lattice has the lowest atomic packing fraction of only 34%, compared to 74% (FCC, HCP), 68% (BCC) and 56% (Simple Cubic) lattices. Thus diamond cubic lattice has 66% of the empty space, which, if utilized cleverly, can lead to higher hardness.  

The diamond cubic unit cell consists of four tetradedra with central atoms, which have number density of atoms of 16/a3, and four missing tetrahedra alternately. These four missing tetrahedra average out the number density of atoms to 8/a3. By using the diamond tetrahedron as the basic structural unit, we able to create novel Q-diamond and Q-carbon based materials with much higher (>60%) number density of atoms than diamond and achieve considerably higher hardness as much as 70% higher than that of diamond.

Final Outcomes:

A new paradigm in designing ultrahard materials has been demonstrated with a proof-of-concept.  In this approach, the basic structural unit is pure or doped carbon tetrahedra with strongly bonded covalent bonds. Since the number density of atoms in a carbon tetrahedron is 16/a3 compared to 8/a3 for diamond cubic lattice (a = lattice constant of diamond), it is possible to achieve higher (>60%) than that of diamond by packing them randomly. Since the bulk modulus scales with the number density of atoms, these materials can have higher (>60%) bulk modulus and hardness than that of diamond. The hardness also requires low Poisson’s ratio, these new materials maintain Poisson’s ratio, similar to that of diamond in view of the similarity in covalent bonding.

The carbon layers (pure and doped) are melted by high-power nanosecond Excimer laser pulses. Upon melting carbon atoms in metallic state are compacted. In the metallic state electrons are delocalized with high mobility. During undercooling, the localization of electrons begins and their mobility starts to decrease, when the distance between atoms starts to increase. When this distance d increases from 1.54 to 2.34 in <110> direction, the localization is complete, leading to formation of covalent sigma σ bonds. The diamond tetrahedron is formed when two atoms in <1-10> direction undergo a similar transition. The formation of diamond tetrahedron in the undercooled state is critical to the formation of phase pure diamond or Q-carbon. The diamond phase is formed, when there is enough time for four of these diamond tetrahedra to attach along <110> and <1-10> directions. If there is not enough time for four of these diamond tetrahedra to attach systematically, Q-carbon is formed where diamond tetrahedra are packed randomly.

Depending upon the available time, we form distinct phases of Q-carbon based upon the number of tetrahedra involved in the basic structural unit. When two tetrahedra as a unit are packed randomly, we form Q2 phase. When three of these tetrahedra as a unit are packed randomly, we form Q1 phase. When a single diamond tetrahedron acts as a unit due to limited time in the undercooled state, we form a Q3 phase, where individual tetrahedron can be packed with a packing efficiency of >80%. This phase transformation in carbon occurs in the undercooled state, but it is similar to semiconductor to metal (SMT) phase transformation in vanadium oxide (VO2) in solid state. In this case, vanadium atoms undergo periodic fluctuation in V-V separation along the c-axis with decreasing temperature, which leads to localization of electrons and transformation to semiconducting state at 340K.

abstractText:
In the software industry, hundreds of programming languages exist, many of which programmers are expected to be proficient in. The common assumption has been that once a programmer knows one language, they can leverage concepts and knowledge already learned and easily pick up another programming language. Unfortunately, empirical studies find this process to be error-prone and ineffective due to imprecise mismatches between concepts and expressions across programming languages. This project develops techniques to ease the acquisition of knowledge for new programming languages by identifying and explaining how the behaviors of code in different languages relate. The anticipated result is that programmers will learn new languages faster and write code with fewer bugs. Beyond the general benefit of better-educated programmers, techniques for teaching computer programming are important in particular because programming is a crucial skill for a digitally literate society.

This project will develop techniques to automatically identify incapabilities and potential misconceptions between two programming languages. Two main research tasks will be investigated for this project. The first task is to develop an approach for automatically identifying clusters of similar code based on dynamic behavior, likely invariants, observed side effects, and performance. Behavioral clusters are formed from snippets in multiple languages that produce the same outputs on the same inputs. Likely invariants from observed behavior are used to describe similarities and differences. The second task is to develop a technique to identify misconceptions that emerge when a programmer assumes code should behave the same but it does not. To identify misconceptions, the technique leverages the behavior clusters and characterizations from the code similarity analysis; code that looks similar but behaves differently in overt (behavior) or insidious (performance, side effects) ways are candidates. The technique will rank misconceptions based on probability of appearing and likely impact.  Finally, the technique will use invariants, behavior, side effects and performance to form automated explanations of behavioral similarities and differences. Finally, these techniques and explanations will be applied for the benefit of two groups of real programmers: transfer students who know one language and need to learn a new one, and data scientists who work with many programming languages to complete their tasks. For programmers learning a new language, in student, professional, or hobby capacities, this work aims to increase the speed and reliability with which they acquire knowledge of the programming language.

abstractText:
This research project will develop statistical methods for the analysis of high-resolution data arising from social media applications. Technological growth has made possible the accumulation of data from social media platforms at unprecedented speed and volume. However, current methods for analyzing these data either lack interpretability, are computationally intense, or require a rigid data regimen. This project will use a flexible modeling framework to extract relevant information on a user's behavior. Although the project primarily will focus on Twitter data, the methods to be developed will be applicable to other social media data, such as Facebook, Instagram, Reddit, or TikTok, or any form of digital interaction. The results of this research will help managers, policymakers, and stakeholders better understand the types of actors they are interacting with on social media. The methods and code created by this project will be made publicly available. The investigators will mentor undergraduate and graduate students and interact with K12 students who are interested in using valid statistical approaches to solve problems arising in online social media.

This research project will develop statistical methods for binary and categorical functional data structures. The standard analysis of functional data relies fundamentally on the assumption that the intrinsic functions are continuous over the compact interval. The complexity of social media data, however, requires different assumptions. A Twitter user's posting pattern can be defined as a time series of some feature of the posting activity. The user's data then can be viewed as a binary-valued or categorical-valued random function defined over a time domain and observed at a fine grid point. The project will develop classification methods for non-continuous functional data, propose computationally efficient estimation algorithms, and study their theoretical properties. The methods to be developed will be extended to adapt to multiple binary-valued or categorical-valued curves per subject, acquired in a longitudinal design, as well as to account for additional covariate information. Regression models with categorical-valued functional covariates and their associated significance tests also will be developed.

projectOutComesReport:
Advancements in technology have enabled the rapid and large-scale collection of data from social media platforms. Existing methods for analyzing this data often struggle with being either difficult to interpret, computationally demanding, or inflexible in their data requirements. Functional data analysis (FDA) provides a flexible yet interpretable framework for modeling and extracting key features of a user's posting behavior on social media, based on the timing, relevant features of their posts during some specified time interval. This project focused on developing FDA-based methodologies to extract user-specific signals based on their posting behavior on social media platforms. The objectives of this award included 1) developing methods for the classification and clustering of binary (0-1 valued) functional data; ii) extending these methods to repeated 0-1 valued functional data while accounting for additional covariates; and iii) developing significance tests when the covariates are categorical functional data. Throughout the course of the project, we developed innovative statistical methods for modeling, prediction, classification, clustering, and hypothesis testing for binary and categorical functional data. The methods were motivated by an applied to various social media data. Below we summarize our key contributions. 

First, we introduced a flexible framework and computationally efficient methodology for classification and clustering of binary or categorical valued functional data. The proposed methods assume that for each such functional data object, there is a latent smooth (univariate or multivariate) process that completely characterize the observed data, and that given the full latent smooth process, the observations are independent. The techniques are applied to social media study where, in addition to the classification or clustering of social media agents with high accuracy, it allows to gain insights into the posting behavior of the various groups/clusters. The methods have been implemented in R packages available on GitHub and are either published in Computational Statistics and Data Analysis or currently under journal review. 

Second, we extended the framework to handle repeated observations of binary-valued functional data for each user and developed computationally efficient methods that extract the user-specific latent signal. These methods inspired by and applied to Twitter data from accounts monitored over several consecutive days and enabled to characterize the accounts’ daily posting behavior and classify them with high accuracy. The work contributed to a PhD thesis and has resulted in a couple of manuscripts that are currently under journal review. 

Third, the we developed test of hypotheses for logistic regression models with categorical-valued functional covariates to formally examine the impact of specific categories on class membership. We proposed a restricted likelihood ratio test, developed its null asymptotic distribution, and presented a computationally efficient approach to calculate the p-value. This technique was motivated by and applied to social media data from X (formerly Twitter) to examine how public statements made by Starbucks and McDonald's regarding the Israel-Hamas conflict influenced customer opinions. Specifically, we described the customers’ opinion through the sentiment of their tweets (positive, neutral, or negative) over a recent period of time and assessed whether a positive sentiment played a significant role in shifting customer opinions toward the company in response to its stance on the conflict. This work contributed to another PhD thesis and led to a manuscript which will be shortly submitted for journal publication. 

This award provided the PIs with opportunities to integrate the proposed research into educational activities that have had a meaningful impact on society at multiple levels. It enabled the PIs to train high school students in working with and analyzing social media data, fostering early interest and competence in data analytics. The insights gained from this research have been instrumental in writing and securing two additional grants, and have formed the basis for the training of six undergraduate students. Additionally, software developed from this research has been made publicly available on GitHub for wider dissemination. Our findings have been showcased at many conferences in statistics and social media-related, contributing to the professional development of attendees and influencing the discussions within the field. The results of this research are also being disseminated through publications in major journals ensuring ongoing visibility and impact.

abstractText:
Work involving human-robot collaboration is an increasingly prevalent work configuration in U.S. manufacturing industries. Since co-robots and workers perform tasks in close proximity, it is not an option to isolate workers from co-robots to avoid accidents, as has been the practice in the past. To date, multiple engineering approaches, including limiting robot speed and eliminating sharp features on the robot, have been implemented in industrial co-robot design to promote the safety of workers. However, the overall risk in human-robot collaboration remains a concern because human workers have limited experience working with co-robot teammates. This award supports fundamental research to provide the new knowledge needed to develop intervention methods to promote the safety awareness and mental health of workers during human-robot collaborations. As the market for collaborative robots is expected to rapidly grow in the next decade, results from this research will benefit workplace safety in the U.S. The research involves multiple disciplines, including occupational safety, cognitive science, computer vision, operations research, and production automation. This multidisciplinary approach will help broaden participation of underrepresented groups in research and strengthen engineering and safety education.

Psychological evidence has revealed that monotonous human-robot collaboration tasks can lead to decreased safety awareness. Human-robot collaboration can also increase workers’ greater mental health risks, as workers treat co-robots as social entities. This research systematically investigates workers' situational awareness and mental stress states in response to interactions with co-robots. The research team will investigate algorithms that interpret video images to enable co-robots to recognize workers' situational awareness and mental stress, thereby enabling the co-robot to perform safety interventions without increasing the mental stress of their human coworkers. Experiments with co-robots will be conducted to evaluate the performance and implementation feasibility of the safety intervention methods.

projectOutComesReport:
Work-related musculoskeletal disorders and the increasing integration of robots into the workplace represent two of the most pressing challenges and opportunities for worker health and safety in recent years. This project combined expertise in human factors, machine learning, and robotics to explore new methods for preventing injuries, improving human well-being, and building trust in emerging human-robot collaboration systems.

One line of research examined the human side of robot integration in occupational settings. By combining robot control with large language models, this work identified strategies to reduce mental stress and enhance user trust in robotic systems. Robots enhanced by language models improved task efficiency, lowered cognitive workload, and fostered trust by enabling workers to communicate through natural language. Experimental studies further revealed that simpler interaction modes, such as verbal or button-based controls, placed less stress on workers than more complex gesture-based inputs. Additional investigations focused on robot behaviors and anthropomorphic features, including approach speed, movement trajectory, facial display, and voice type, that influence workers’ emotional responses and perceptions of safety. These studies showed that slower, predictable movements and thoughtfully designed social features can reduce physiological stress and improve collaboration effectiveness. Collectively, these contributions strengthen the intellectual foundation for human-centered, AI-enabled workplace safety systems that are both technically effective and responsive to human well-being.

The second line of research tackled the limitations of data-driven human factors studies, which are often constrained by small or imbalanced datasets and strict privacy requirements. To address these challenges, the project advanced generative modeling, federated learning, and transfer learning techniques to produce realistic representations of human behaviors data. Diffusion-based models were created to predict workers’ postures with high anatomical validity, surpassing earlier approaches in both accuracy and variability. Federated learning frameworks showed how multiple organizations can collaborate to train models for worker stress detection and activity recognition without exchanging raw data, ensuring privacy protection. Transfer learning methods further improved the adaptability of these models, increased classification accuracy, and substantially reduced training time, offering practical solutions for applying human factor research in settings where data are limited.

The broader impacts of this project reach across science, industry, and society. By developing tools for more accurate risk assessment and privacy-preserving data analysis, the research helps industries better prevent work-related musculoskeletal disorders and safely adopt collaborative robots that support worker well-being. Incorporating language models into robotics opens new possibilities for creating robots that communicate naturally with workers, including those without advanced technical training. This promotes safer and more effective use of automation in warehouses, factories, and service industries. In addition, the project contributed to education and workforce development by preparing graduate students in advanced areas of AI, robotics, and human factors, while sharing results through publications, conferences, and outreach efforts that expand participation in STEM.

In sum, this project advanced the science of human factors by deepening the understanding of safety in human-robot collaboration through both empirical studies and theoretical advances in analytical methods. The outcomes include new generative models for producing and sharing human factors data, design principles for low-stress human-robot interactions, and evidence that large language models can improve trust and efficiency in robotic partnerships. Taken together, these findings promote the development of safer and healthier workplaces in an era of rapid technological change.

abstractText:
This Major Research Instrumentation (MRI) award will support the acquisition of a diffusion bonding hot press furnace (furnace) with high-temperature capabilities to enhance research and education at North Carolina State University (NCSU) and area universities and industries. The furnace will  catalyze fundamental research on new manufacturing processes and materials-- leading to enhanced performance, safety and efficiency for products ranging from aircraft to biomedical devices. The furnace will be integrated into courses on advanced materials and manufacturing and used for outreach activities in additive manufacturing, including a Manufacturing Summer Camp for high school and middle school students.  It will help to foster collaborative efforts with industry and to give students exposure to research experiences in partnership with industry.

The furnace will enable fundamental studies to understand the effect of processing parameters on the performance of selected material systems, which range from metal foams to high temperature multifunctional ceramic sensors and from high entropy alloys to reinforced Ti matrix composites. Potentially transformative research on composite metal foam technology can enable higher energy absorption, excellent radiation shielding, blast resistance, and good thermal insulation. This instrument will allow the fabrication of the metal foams more consistently and reliably at much larger and testable scales.  The research on the development of high temperature sensors would be potentially transformative by allowing the microstructure and properties of the sensors to be controlled through the control of their thermal history. There is a great need for such multifunctional ceramics at ultrahigh temperatures for structural health monitoring.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

abstractText:
A team of researchers will undertake research to study the organization of small-scale, village-based societies and, especially, resistance to the process of state formation. Archaeologists have long been interested in documenting and explaining the origins of the state, but attention has recently shifted toward societies that explicitly sought to prevent state formation, that is, to prevent the accumulation of wealth, power, and authority in the hands of any particular individual or group. Understanding how these intentionally small-scale, decentralized, and egalitarian societies operated can yield new insight into the diverse forms of governance organization that have developed, persisted, and thrived alongside states. Archaeology offers the only scientific means of glimpsing the operation of such organization in prehistory. Given its focus on the physical remains left behind by past societies, archaeology also draws attention to the spaces, places, and objects that helped people construct and maintain specific governance systems. 

The research team will use archaeological evidence for food production, craft production, community organization, burial practices, symbolic representations, and trade to study governance organization in a village-based, egalitarian society contemporary with and in close proximity to the classic centers of state formation. Excavations are designed to collect evidence for the governance of village life in one small settlement and thereby provide a glimpse into the operation of such a small-scale, locally organized, and deliberately maintained alternative to the state. The research will consist of a three-year program of archaeological data collection and analysis that includes study of ceramic, lithic, metallurgical, architectural, zooarchaeological, palaeobotanical, osteological, and geoarchaeological remains. Drawing on these diverse data sets, the project will provide a new perspective on the deep history of efforts to build and maintain more equitable social systems. It will also contribute to international education, training, cultural heritage preservation, and human resource development.

This award from the Major Research Instrumentation program supports the acquisition of a state-of-the-art focused ion beam /scanning electron microscope outfitted with advanced detectors and automation tools.  The instrument enables and supports a diverse range of research projects and programs, within academia and industry, that involve three-dimensional, multi-modal characterization and patterning of microstructures. Such three-dimensional analysis is particularly important for developing materials processing strategies for additive manufacturing and for understanding mechanisms leading to material degradation and failure.  In addition, the nanopatterning capabilities of the instrument provide precision engineering of novel nanometer-scale optical and mechanical devices. The location of the instrument within the Research Triangle Nanotechnology Network, a node of the NSF National Nanotechnology Coordinated Infrastructure (NNCI), provides enhanced access to researchers from across the nation, impacting local universities, not-for-profit institutions and industries. The instrument will be integrated into the curriculum developed under an NSF-funded National Research Traineeship program, which brings together the materials science, statistics and machine learning communities to develop new approaches to materials informatics research. Workshops and training modules will be developed to broaden participation from minority institutions and to educate a new generation of researchers at the intersection of statistics and materials science.  

This award supports the acquisition of an inductively coupled plasma (ICP) multi-ion source focused-ion beam/ scanning electron microscope (pFIB/SEM) to support the ongoing and future research of numerous faculty, postdoctoral and student researchers from across five academic departments at North Carolina State University and regional universities. In addition, the instrument will be broadly utilized by other academic and industry research communities via the Research Triangle Nanotechnology Network, a node of the NSF National Nanotechnology Coordinated Infrastructure (NNCI). The instrument is outfitted specifically for statistically meaningful quantitative characterization of material microstructures in three dimensions across length scales from nano meter to millimeter. The coupling of automation tools with the rapid sputtering rates unlocks the ability to: 1) study material properties governed by complex hierarchical material microstructures, 2) study three dimensional microstructures in materials that would be susceptible to artifacts from ion implantation using conventional Ga ion sources, and 3) pattern large area yet high fidelity (nanometer-scale resolution) patterns in a variety of materials. The broader impacts of the infrastructure lie in leveraging the unique capabilities of the North Carolina State Analytical Instrumentation Facility in training a diverse user-base and in developing education modules at the graduate, undergraduate and K-12 levels.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

abstractText:
Improving student success in subject domains that serve as gateway courses to STEM careers, such as chemistry and math, is of great interest. These subjects are difficult to teach and learn, partly because they involve a complex network of interconnected knowledge. Current online instructional materials generally follow a linear sequence, tracing a single predetermined pathway through the knowledge network. The CyberBook technology developed in this project instead guides students through the knowledge network along pathways chosen to optimize their learning of both the individual concepts and the relations between these concepts. The pathways adapt to individual students, with information gathered from a student’s interaction with the online materials to select a pathway that is optimal for that individual student. Although the primary focus is on chemistry and mathematics, the approach can be applied to other STEM domains. CyberBook combines traditional online courseware with intelligent tutoring systems. It also provides a research platform for learning scientists to conduct studies on how students learn. Beyond learning science, the proposed research has the potential to advance the literature on education (both domain-specific and domain-general), educational data mining, and artificial intelligence in education. 

This project will develop several advanced learning-engineering methods to facilitate the creation of high-quality and effective online courseware: (1) an application of reinforcement learning to compute optimal sequencing of topics and scaffolding, (2) a text-mining method to automatically discover skills to be learned from text in written instructions and assessments, (3) a web browser-based method to rapidly create intelligent tutoring systems and seamlessly integrate them into online courseware, and (4) an application of reinforcement learning for an evidence-based quality control for online courseware content. As a proof of concept, instances of CyberBook for a college level chemistry (stoichiometry) and high school math (coordinate geometry) will be created. To validate the feasibility of implementation, the proposed learning engineering methods will be applied to two existing online course platforms—Open Learning Initiative and Open edX. The effectiveness of the proposed intervention will be measured through a pilot evaluation study at the partner institutions.

projectOutComesReport:
The primary goal of this project is to develop advanced learning-engineering methods to facilitate the creation of high-quality, effective online courseware. We have developed three key technologies: (1) A text-mining method to automatically discover latent skills from written instructions and assessments in the courseware. (2) An authoring method that allows for the rapid creation of an intelligent tutoring system on a standard web browser by interactively teaching an AI agent (called SimStudent). (3) A quality-assurance method that identifies key elements of the online courseware by applying reinforcement-learning techniques to actual student learning log data. These methods are platform-independent and have been applied to two existing platforms: Open edX and the Open Learning Initiative. We call the resulting extended online courseware platform “CyberBook.”

As a proof of concept, we created two instances of CyberBook: one for college-level chemistry (stoichiometry) and another for high school math (coordinate geometry). The validity of the text-mining method (called SMART) was empirically tested on two existing courses at the Open Learning Initiative. The model validation demonstrated that the latent skills discovered by SMART accurately predicted students’ performance on formative assessment questions, supporting the validity of the latent skills identified by the method. Additionally, the study demonstrated that the predictions made using the latent skills discovered by SMART were as accurate as those made using latent skills suggested by experienced instructors. The web-browser based authoring tool (called WATSON) was used to create cognitive tutors for the CyberBook courseware for coordinate geometry. An empirical study to evaluate performance of WATSON showed that the cognitive tutors created by WATSON was able to accurately judge the correctness of the student solutions. The quality-assurance tool (called RAFINE) was evaluated using synthetic data that the investigators generated for hypothetical online courseware. The results showed that over 90% of ineffective instructional components were correctly identified as ineffective on average. Those results suggest that the learning-engineering methods that the investigators have developed has a high potential to facilitate the creation of high-quality, effective yet pragmatic online courseware.

abstractText:
In this project, the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on household food insecurity are investigated.  Food insecurity rates in the United States have more than doubled as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic.  Food insecurity rates also vary widely across place, with state averages ranging from 14 percent to 32 percent.  Researchers investigate how variations in social context and official responses to the pandemic affect families’ ability to prevent or cope with food insecurity by documenting the ways the pandemic has affected how families shop for food, cook, and eat.  Results have implications for how community and governmental groups can develop more responsive and equitable responses to a range of crises.

To identify the key contextual and official response variables that exacerbate or reduce place-based disparities in food insecurity, 160 semi-structured interviews are conducted and photovoice data are collected with a diverse group of poor and working-class families in four rural and four urban counties across four U.S. states. The four states have been selected to ensure variations in severity of COVID-19 outbreaks and in state responses. The data are analyzed to understand how experiences of food insecurity vary between and within states, and how variations in social context and official food directives affect whether and how people are able to buffer the impacts of food insecurity.

projectOutComesReport:
Food insecurity in the United States rose dramatically at the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. However, by the end of 2020, rates had fallen to pre-pandemic levels, and overall food insecurity did not significantly increase between 2020 and 2021. Our qualitative, multi-sited study of people's experiences of food insecurity during the pandemic offers insight into why. In 2020 and 2021, we conducted two rounds of semi-structured interviews in rural and urban counties in five states. Our research shows how safety net programs that were expanded or created during the pandemic-- including SNAP, P-EBT, school meal programs, and the Child Tax Credit-- improved many households' access to food. By removing administrative burdens, boosting benefit levels, and making some benefits universal (rather than means-tested), pandemic policies reduced stigma and delivered resources quickly and effectively. At the same time, benefits were not equally available to all. Some groups were excluded by design, and uncertainty about when benefits would arrive and how long they would last contributed to stress and anxiety. In addition, our research shows how participants' broader social context and structural inequalities shaped their experiences of food insecurity and the resources they had access to. Access varied by state, with some states taking far longer to implement programs and offering fewer benefits, which in turn contributes to inequality. Rurality also influenced access to food resources (particularly emergency food providers). Our research illustrates the importance of safety net programs that can be mobilized quickly and widely, whether in a pandemic or admidst the regular interruptions of everyday life.

abstractText:
Student interest and affect play critical roles in shaping how individuals learn. Interest impacts student engagement with scientific ideas and practices, student learning outcomes, and the ability to set goals and self-regulate. Student interest is also a well-known precursor to STEM career development. Over the past several years, research on affect-sensitive learning environments has enabled data-rich investigations into the affective dynamics of student learning. However, designing adaptive learning environments that respond effectively to student affect is a key gap in the research. Recent developments in multimodal affect recognition and adaptive learning technologies have set the stage for the creation of affect-responsive interventions to support student learning, engagement, and critically, the development of science interest. This project centers on the design, development, and investigation of a multimodal affect-sensitive learning environment to enhance middle school students’ science learning, engagement, and interest in science. The project will investigate the relationship between student affect and interest in science, enabling the development of methods to support learning and interest development through multimodal, affect-sensitive interventions within an inquiry-based science learning environment. It is anticipated that the project will advance the national goal of providing effective, engaging science learning experiences for all students.

With the overarching goal of developing methods and adaptive learning technologies that enable improved STEM education, the project has two major objectives: The first objective is to design, develop, and refine an affect-sensitive learning environment based on multimodal neural architectures to generate and sustain student interest in inquiry-based science learning. A suite of physical hardware sensors to capture rich multi-channel data (facial expression, eye gaze, posture, gesture, interaction trace logs) combined with quantitative observations of student affect and behavioral engagement (i.e., an established protocol for observations) will be utilized to train multimodal recurrent neural network-based models of student affect recognition. These models will drive adaptive interventions to guide students toward engaged problem solving by triggering and maintaining student interest in science inquiry. The affect-sensitive interventions will be integrated with Crystal Island, an inquiry-based learning environment for middle school science education. The second objective is to investigate the impact of the multimodal affect-sensitive learning environment on student learning, engagement, and interest in science. A culminating study with middle school students will examine the impact of these designs, comparing the multimodal affect-sensitive learning environment to a baseline environment without affect-sensitive interventions. This comparison will test the effectiveness of the learning environment in fostering enhanced learning and interest outcomes across a diverse range of learners, examining measures of knowledge, engagement, and interest, including interest in science and interest in STEM careers. The resulting findings will yield significant contributions to both theory and practice in student interest development and produce an empirical account of the effectiveness of multimodal neural architectures for modeling and responding to student affect.
