Final Project Outcomes Report

Title: Enhancing Science Learning through Multimodal, Affect-Sensitive Game-Based Learning Environments

This project explored how students' emotions, interest, and engagement during science learning can be better understood and supported through advanced technologies. The team designed and studied an innovative learning environment that uses affect-sensitive artificial intelligence (AI) to recognize and respond to middle school students’ emotions while they engage in science inquiry.

The research focused on a game-based learning environment called Crystal Island, where students solve a mystery by exploring a virtual world and applying science concepts. The project added new capabilities to Crystal Island that allow it to detect students’ emotional states—such as boredom, frustration, or curiosity—using a combination of data sources like facial expressions, in-game behaviors, and self-reported feelings. These affect-sensitive models help the system better support student learning by adapting the experience based on how students are feeling in real time.

What Was Accomplished

The project had two main goals: (1) to create a multimodal system that detects and responds to student emotions during science learning, and (2) to study how this system impacts student learning, engagement, and interest in science.

Key accomplishments included:

  • Developing advanced AI models that detect student emotions using both self-reports and trained human observations. These models were able to identify patterns in how students transition between different emotional states over time.

  • Identifying student learning "archetypes"—patterns of behavior that distinguish different types of learners. For example, some students spent more time exploring and testing ideas, while others showed signs of disengagement or rushed through tasks. These archetypes helped researchers understand how emotions and behaviors relate to learning outcomes and motivation.

  • Building new tools to explain students’ emotions, not just detect them. For example, if a student felt confused, the system could also infer whether that confusion came from finding the material either too easy or too hard. This kind of understanding could help future systems give more personalized support.

  • Applying large language models to make predictions about student emotions and their attributions, based on gameplay data, expanding the potential of AI to understand and support students in more sophisticated ways.

  • Creating the SDVET model, a new theoretical framework that explains how emotions during learning are shaped by students’ skills, perceived task difficulty, sense of value, confidence, and time. This model can help educators and designers to better interpret students’ in-the-moment affective experiences and how they might be used to improve learning.

Impacts and Broader Contributions

This project contributes to the growing field of affective computing in education—using technology to sense and respond to students’ feelings in ways that support learning. The work has produced insights about how emotion, motivation, and behavior interact in game-based learning environments, particularly for middle school students learning science.

The findings suggest that frustration and confusion, when managed well, can be productive emotions that contribute to learning. However, persistent boredom often signaled disengagement and lower learning outcomes. Understanding these patterns can help developers create learning tools that better support emotional and cognitive engagement.

Beyond the technical advances, the project emphasized collaboration between researchers, educators, and schools. The team partnered with several middle schools in North Carolina, involving teachers and students in the research and using their input to refine the learning environment.

The project also made substantial contributions to workforce development. Graduate students and early-career scholars from groups underrepresented in STEM gained experience in cutting-edge educational research, including AI modeling, data analysis, and classroom studies. All of these students authored or co-authored peer-reviewed publications and one has since moved into tenure-track faculty positions or continued advanced research.

Dissemination

The team presented their findings at major international conferences, including the International Conference on Educational Data Mining, the Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference, and the ACM Computer Science Education Symposium. Publications appeared in leading journals such as the Journal of Science Education and Technology, helping to share results with researchers and practitioners alike.

The tools, models, and insights developed through this project offer a foundation for future work in personalized learning, educational games, and affective computing. The team’s continued partnerships with school districts and academic collaborators ensure that the impact of the project will extend well beyond its formal end.

abstractText:
Land surface albedo is the fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected by the land surface. It is an essential climate variable as identified by the Global Climate Observing System. An international effort involving institutions from the USA, European Union, Japan, Switzerland and Korea is dedicated to obtaining geostationary images from five different satellites. Those satellites have overlapping areas for which two different measures of albedo are retrieved. The project will develop blended global albedo products that account for the discrepancies between the different retrievals and quantify the uncertainty in the resulting albedo values using probabilities. The project will leverage the expertise of two PIs to develop state of the art methods that can capture the variability in time and space of climate variables that are observed from a constellation of geostationary satellites, like cloud characteristics, wind speed and direction, snow cover, and precipitation, among others. 

The project will contribute geostatistical methods with a model-based approach to analyze, interpolate and make inferences for a multivariate spatial field, featuring a non-stationary spatial process, indexed in a continuous space. The scalability is achieved thanks to a local neighborhood conditioning structure. Computations will be performed fast and concurrently, satisfying global coherence through a hierarchical structure. The model-based nature of the proposed approach allows to account for complex observational errors, perform non-homogeneous multivariate spatial regression, and combine observations obtained at different levels of spatial aggregation. Extensions to spatio-temporal models are seamlessly obtained incorporating space-time interactions within a parsimonious hierarchical model.

projectOutComesReport:
This project seeks to obtain state of the art climate data products from several, partially overlapping, geostationary satellites. The project aims to produce ensembles of gridded fields that result from combining the observations of the different satellites and that reflect the main predictive uncertainties. In order to obtain the desired data products, the proposed research will advance the field of geostatistics by developing probabilistic methods for multivariate, nonstationary fields in space and space-time. The statistical methods considered in this project put emphasis on computational approaches that can leverage the availability of multi-processors and multi-threading to obtain speed and scalability. 

During the first year of the project we were able to reach the following achievements:

(a) Establish frequent and effective communication between the PIs. We conducted bi-weekly meetings via videoconference.

(b) Make key information available. From the satellite retrievals available to PI Matthews, we selected the daily data for satellites GOES-75 and GOES-135 corresponding to January and July of the year 2000. The idea is to explore the characteristic of albedo under winter and summer conditions.

(c) Make a computational platform available. PI Sanso worked to install the software needed to ingest, process and analyse the data from the satellite restrievals in the computers and clusters available in the network of the Basking School of Engineering of UCSC.

(d) Perfom a descriptive analysis of the data and assess the computational needs with particular emphasis on the exploration of the discrepancy between the two satellites.

(e) Obtain preliminary results from two different models. We fitted a model based on multi-resolution representation of spatial fields, as well as model based on nearest neighbors to the area corresponding to the continental US.

Significant outcomes include:

(a) Kelsey Blackstone, MS student in the program of Statistical Science at UCSC completed her MS project under the supervision of PI Sanso. The title of the thesis is "Using Multi-resolution Process Convolutions to Model Land-Surface Albedo". Kelsey's work was framed by the topic of the project.

(b) Isabelle Grenier, PhD student in the program of Statistical Science at UCSC is working on a PhD dissertation on the development of scalable spatial geostatistical models is fully within the scope of the project. She published a paper on distributed methods to fit a geostatistical model based on nearest neighborhood.

abstractText:
This grant will advance the national prosperity and security through a scientific understanding of fluid-structure interactions that will advance the fields of aerodynamics, structural dynamics, and vibration control favorable for future high-efficiency aircraft, extended endurance in swarms of swimming or flying robots, enhanced wind and hydrokinetic energy generation, and protection of infrastructure like bridges and pipelines from fatigue damage due to wind and water flows. This award supports fundamental research on modifying and controlling fluid-structure interactions by way of introducing prescribed flow disturbances from an upstream disturbance generator. Depending on the application, it may be desirable to suppress a flutter instability or attenuate oscillations (as in an aircraft wing or turbine blade), increase the amplitude of oscillations (as in an oscillating flow energy harvester), or reshape an oscillation to beneficially affect fluid-structure energy transfer (as in a swarm of swimming or flying robots synchronizing to minimize energy consumption). The approach studied here will enable any of these distinct behaviors to be generated on-demand. The multi-disciplinary approach, and the education activities at the middle school through doctoral levels, will help broaden the participation of underrepresented groups in research and positively impact engineering education.

The objective of this project is to enable distinct aeroelastic system behaviors including equilibrium stabilization / destabilization or limit cycle oscillation amplitude increase / decrease to be created, controlled, and modified on-demand by prescribing aerodynamic disturbances that interact with a target aeroelastic wing. The project aims to understand, model, and formulate control approaches for aeroelastic wings being affected by canonical flow disturbances such as convecting vortices. The first goal is to understand and map the spatiotemporal relationships between incoming flow disturbances and the unsteady aerodynamic forces and moments on a wing using a custom discrete vortex method with a model for external flow disturbances (LDVM-Disturbance) and wind tunnel experiments for validation. A second goal is to establish the effects of incoming flow disturbance topology, strength, frequency content, and phasing on the stability and nonlinear oscillation behavior of an aeroelastic wing. This will be investigated in simulation by coupling the LDVM-Disturbance model with an aeroelastic structural dynamics model, and in validation experiments by measuring the response of an aeroelastic wing section downstream of an actuated disturbance generator. A third goal is to create a sequence of feed-forward system inversions that allows required disturbance generator motions to be determined to produce desired responses in the downstream aeroelastic wing. The results will be used to demonstrate open-loop control of aeroelastic stability and oscillation phenomena in wind tunnel experiments.

projectOutComesReport:
Overview: This project has enhanced understanding of the stability, dynamics, motions, and control of aeroelastic structures interacting with upstream flow disturbances. Aeroelastic structures, which are defined as flexible bodies subject to external aerodynamic or hydrodynamic forces, can be found in a range of applications from aircraft wings, to bridge decks, to heat exchangers, to bird wings and fish fins. Establishing methods to controllably suppress or enhance oscillations in these structures can improve safety and flight performance in aircraft, enable new types of wind or underwater energy generation, or improve energy efficiency of swimming robots. As part of the effort, the work has studied and characterized pitch-oscillating cylinders with attached splitter plates as controllable flow disturbance generators and created nonlinear simulation methods for aeroelastic wings using low-order, unsteady aerodynamics models capable of modeling large amplitude motions and vortex interactions. We have used prescribed flow disturbances, namely vortex wakes of the disturbance generator, to excite or annihilate nonlinear limit cycle oscillations (LCOs) on-demand in an aeroelastic wing. We have also studied the effects of vortex frequency and phase on the range of conditions over which LCOs are possible and how quickly those LCOs can be annihilated. Additionally, simulations through both computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and low-order methods have allowed us to study the formation of vortices and model their behavior across a range of conditions. The low-order methods also present a fast modelling framework with will prove useful in further applications in aeroelastic research, especially in situations where aeroelasticity is one part of a larger analytical or control framework.

Intellectual Merit: This research effort has made the following contributions to the scientific and engineering community:

  • We developed and implemented a variable frequency disturbance generator (VFDG) which can produced a tailored vortex wake with a range of shedding frequencies.
  • We demonstrated amplitude modulation in aeroelastic wing limit cycle oscillations (LCOs) due to prescribed impinging vortices at frequencies near the inherent LCO frequency of the wing.
  • We demonstrated LCO excitation and annihilation in an aeroelastic wing using prescribed impinging vortices from an upstream disturbance generator.
  • We characterized the relationship between vortex frequency and phase and the ability to annihilate LCOs in an aeroelastic wing.
  • We developed a low-order model that was shown to successfully predict the aeroelastic wing limit-cycle oscillation characteristics with comparable results to our experimental measurements.
  • We built a recurrent neural network to identify and predict the aeroelastic state of a wing using experimental data gathered from an aeroelastic wing exposed to incoming flow disturbances.
  • We used CFD to study the effects of different splitter plate lengths attached to oscillating cylinders on wake formation, vortex strength, and lift and drag enhancement.

Broader Impacts: This project benefits society through STEM outreach and educational activities carried out by the PIs’ labs including:

  • Development of aeroelasticity educational modules to be used in conjunction with the NCSU MAE summer camps hosted each year on NCSU’s Centennial Campus.
  • Development and instruction of a virtual engineering summer camp which was attended by over 70 high school students during the summer of 2021.
  • Provided research experience and mentoring to one post-doc student, six graduate students, nine undergraduate students, and ten high school students.
  • Worked with a local high school student through a mentorship program with the North Carolina School of Science and Math (NCSSM), where they participated in semester-long research internships and received hands-on training to design and fabricate conceptual prototypes.

The project also benefits society by creating a new mechanism for suppressing, enhancing, or altering aeroelastic interactions as desired in a variety of engineered systems. This could lead to aircraft with lighter weight and more efficient wing designs, which would reduce emissions from air transportation, bridges and buildings that are better protected from damaging wind and water flows in storms, more efficient and cost-competitive wind and hydrokinetic power devices, and groups of flying or swimming robots with extended range and endurance for disaster response missions like mapping oil spills or delivering medical supplies to impassable regions.

abstractText:
Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a skin disease caused by a parasitic infection, which affects up to one million people each year. There are many shortcomings to current drug treatments for this disease, including hearing loss and kidney damage. The goal of this joint North Carolina State University (NCSU) and Ohio State University (OSU) project is to understand the unique functionality of a microscale biosystem containing microneedle array that (a) emits light from an optical component and subsequently (b) provides local release of a drug with antiparasitic activity. This project seeks to better understand a new type of microscale device technology that both (a) uses focused light to treat the parasitic infection and (b) uses a small pump to deliver an antiparasitic drug directly to the site of infection. Functionality of the novel device that provides both light therapy and drug therapy will be compared with devices that provide either light therapy or drug therapy alone. Goal of the project is to evaluate the feasibility of the multimodal technology to enhance treatment efficiency by comparing with different types of therapies. Graduate students will be trained in fiber optics and microfabrication of functional biosystems technologies   and will be mentored in effective methods for teaching large groups. The PI will disseminate results from the project through quarterly Science Saturday lectures and hands-on activities at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences. The technical benefit of this project lies in forming the basis for multimodal technology that will have significant impact on new types of precise treatments for cancer and other diseases.

The intellectual merit associated with this project involves developing a better understanding of multimodal technologies, which include two or more types of pharmacologic therapy and/or device-based therapy; this technology is considered an emerging area of engineering research. Objective 1 will involve fabrication of a microscale biosystem containing optical fibers, a pump, and a microneedle array. Objective 2 will involve testing and validation of the microscale biosystem. Objective 1 and 2 will be performed at NCSU. Objective 3 will involve evaluation of the efficacy of the microscale biosystem in which optical functionality and drug delivery functionality are provided together; comparisons of this multimodal approach to drug therapy alone and light therapy alone will be performed at OSU. The feasibility study supported by this project will enable submission of a full proposal on comprehensively understanding the design of the microscale biosystem. It is anticipated that this microscale biosystem can provide a more effective treatment of cutaneous leishmaniasis than conventional drug therapy, which is associated with repeated dosing, long treatment times, and toxicity.

projectOutComesReport:
This EAGER project, which was performed by North Carolina State University (NCSU) and The Ohio State University (OSU), examined the development of a light-integrated multimodal microscale biosystem for transdermal delivery of amphotericin B to treat cutaneous leishmaniasis. It should be noted that microneedles offer several benefits for antileishmanial and antiparasitic therapy, including low manufacturing cost, ease of use, absence of pain, and minimization of trauma at the treatment site. 

In one study, microneedles were loaded for the delivery of amphotericin B, the gold standard therapy for cutaneous leishmaniasis and fungal infections. One of the main drawbacks of conventional polymeric microneedles is their limited capability for effectively loading a sufficient amount of a drug. Furthermore, the loading process itself may potentially cause damage or affect the potency of certain drugs. In the paper Machekposhti SA, Kadian S, Vanderwal L, Stafslien S, Narayan RJ. Novel hollow biodegradable microneedle for amphotericin B delivery. MedComm. 2023 Aug;4(4):e321, a previously unexplored form of biodegradable hollow microneedle was successfully described. Creating biodegradable hollow microneedles involved the use of a biodegradable material known as Gantrez® AN 119 BF, which was processed into the desired shape. In order to load the hollow microneedles with a powdered version of the drug amphotericin B, a process was utilized that involved both vacuuming and shaking simultaneously. Through this particular approach, a significantly large quantity of medication was able to be successfully loaded into the microneedles. In order to measure the mechanical properties of the microneedles, nanoindentation and mechanical testing were employed. The technique known as laser confocal microscopy was utilized in order to precisely measure the exact dimensions of the microneedles. The results from antifungal testing revealed that the microneedles containing amphotericin B were effective in inhibiting the growth of Candida albicans.

In another study that is under review by the Informa (Taylor & Francis) journal Drug Delivery, the NCSU and OSU researchers showed that microneedle-based injection of Fungizone/Amphotericin B is an effective treatment for American cutaneous leishmaniasis in a murine model We considered the use of hollow microneedles to directly deliver Amphotericin B to localized cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) lesions. Our hypothesis suggests that this method would effectively inhibit parasite growth without causing any systemic toxicity. A three-by-three array of 1 mm tall stainless steel hollow microneedles was utilized to successfully administer Fungizone/Amphotericin B into the skin. In order to accurately assess the effectiveness of our treatment, we conducted experiments using Leishmania mexicana-infected BALB/c mice as a model. After administering 10 and 20 consecutive days of microneedle treatments, our results demonstrated a significant decrease in parasitic burden in both trials, with the 20-day trial showing particularly promising results in limiting lesion growth compared to the control groups who received a placebo. A notable finding from the 10-day trial was the absence of any increase in blood serum creatinine or blood urea nitrogen levels, suggesting that there was no kidney toxicity. The results of this study have shown potential for use of hollow microneedles for the treatment of cutaneous leishmaniasis. The utilization of these products has the potential to significantly decrease the burden of cutaneous leishmaniasis among those affected by cutraneous leishmaniasis.

We also examined another multimodal microneedle device, which contained sensors. In Kadian S, Kumari P, Sahoo SS, Shukla S, Narayan RJ. Machine learning enabled microneedle-based colorimetric pH sensing patch for wound health monitoring and meat spoilage detection. Microchemical Journal. 2024 Mar 19:110350, our team successfully created a user-friendly and affordable machine learning-powered microneedle-based colorimetric pH sensing patch, which has the potential to transform wound health monitoring. The 3D-printed microneedle array enabled autonomous fluid extraction and pH sensing via surface tension. In order to determine the precise pH level based on the observed color on the pH-test strip, a machine learning model was meticulously developed using a collection of various color images acquired from numerous experiments with known pH solutions. In order to support to the needs of older individuals and those with color blindness, a user-friendly and accessible web application that utilizes the developed machine learning model was implemented. In order to demonstrate the effectiveness of the developed patch, a proof-of-concept study was conducted. Based on the analytical results, the newly created machine learning enabled microneedle-based colorimetric pH sensing patch shows potential for wound health monitoring.

Presentations were delivered at the Society for Biomaterials Annual Meeting, the MS&T Annual Meeting, the MDPI Sensors Webinar Series, as well as invited seminars at CEA-Leti (France), RMIT University (Australia), and Florida State University.

Graduate students at NCSU and OSU received training in microfabrication, biosystem integration, and analytical methods.

The research team provided demonstrations on microneedle fabrication, biosensing, and bioprinting to educators and North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences visitors. These events promoted public engagement with science & engineering topics; moreover, the events sought to inspire interest among the museum visitors in STEM careers.

abstractText:
This project aims to serve the national interest in high-quality STEM education by studying an intervention designed to improve persistence of women in computer science. Engaging all people in learning about STEM, particularly computer science, is important for innovation, global competitiveness, and preparation for future careers that increasingly rely on computing. Women occupy just 28% of STEM jobs and account for only 17% of computer science majors and 21% of engineering majors. These differences in career choices arise partially from gender differences in self-assessment of STEM ability. This project will test whether educational institutions can use a simple intervention to increase the persistence of women in computer science. This intervention consists of email messages to students in introductory computer science courses.  The messages contain contextual information about the student’s performance in class and encouragement regarding their effort and potential. For example, a message might reveal that the student is a top performer in the course and suggest that the student should explore getting involved in undergraduate computer science research.  A pilot study found that changing the wording of a single email could increase women's intentions to stay in computer science by 18%. This project aims to evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention on a larger scale, and determine how to maximize its efficacy.  If successful, the project will provide educational institutions with a simple, easily implemented tool to increase the number of women in computer science fields. This intervention could have positive effects on other groups that face negative stereotypes about their intellectual capacity and ability to succeed in computer sciences, and might be applicable to other STEM disciplines, as well. 
 
This project will use both a field experiment and an online experiment to test the intervention. The field experiment will be conducted across all the introductory computer science courses at a large research-based university. Multivariate analysis will be conducted to determine both the immediate and longitudinal effects of the intervention on self-assessed computer science ability and on persistence in computer science. Qualitative interviews will be conducted with some students in the field experiment to obtain nuanced data about students’ experience with the intervention. The online experiment will use short programming activities and will explore which pieces of contextual information are most effective. This knowledge will be critical for crafting efficient messages that can be used at scale, and for determining methods (other than emails) through which institutions can boost students’ self-assessment and persistence in computer science. Mediation analyses will be used in both the field and online experiments to illuminate the process through which the intervention impacts self-assessed computer science ability, and in turn, persistence. This research is expected to contribute to theoretical and practical knowledge of how institutions can intervene to promote gender equity and to increase knowledge about the social-psychological processes around self-assessments of ability and career choice that reproduce existing gender inequalities.  This project is supported by the NSF Improving Undergraduate STEM Education Program: Education and Human Resources Program, which supports research and development projects to improve the effectiveness of STEM education for all students. Through the Engaged Student Learning track, the program supports the creation, exploration, and implementation of promising practices and tools.

projectOutComesReport:
The U.S. is facing a shortage of professionals with computing skills, which has important implications for innovation, economic progress, and national security. Unfortunately, most efforts to increase the number of students with computing skills are resource intensive and only focus on students already in computing majors. Thus, there is a need for lightweight interventions that focus on students who have not already declared a major or minor in computing. 

To fill this gap, we introduced and evaluated a lightweight career-choice intervention, which brought new students into the field of computing by targeting the career-choice process itself. This intervention focused on assuring top-performing students in non-major computing courses that they had the ability to succeed in computing. This is important because even high-performing students often have an inaccurate assessment of their own ability. This is especially true in computing courses that tend to have lower course grades, and where students often compare themselves unfavorably to peers with prior experience. These self-assessments of ability are notoriously inaccurate but have profound impacts on students’ career decisions. And unlike actual ability, it may be possible to improve students’ self-assessments with minimal effort by giving students contextual information about their performance. We tested our career-choice intervention using a randomized field experiment with top-performing students in introductory, non-major computing courses. We found evidence that our career-choice intervention increased students’ self-assessed ability, professional role confidence, belonging, and intentions to pursue a computing career. We also found evidence that our career-choice intervention doubled the likelihood that students: 1) stated that they will minor in computer science (CS), 2) took another computing course, and 3) applied to be a teaching assistant in a computing course. Lastly, we find evidence supporting our hypothesis for why the intervention worked: it improved students’ self-assessed ability, which in turn increased their intentions to pursue a computing career.

These results were echoed in qualitative interviews conducted with students at the end of the course. We interviewed 59 students about their experiences in computing, their self-assessments of computing ability, and their career choices. Of these students, 29 were in the intervention condition. Without any prompting or mention of the intervention, 11 of them (37.9%) mentioned the emails as being significant to them in some capacity, whether through impacting their self-assessment of ability, encouraging them to apply to be a TA, and/or impacting their decision to take another computing course. We consider the fact that so many students brought up the emails without prompting to be further evidence of the importance of the career-choice intervention, especially given how many emails students receive in a given semester. 


 In sum, this research finds evidence that a lightweight career-choice intervention can bring new students into computing, highlights the importance of self-assessments in the career-choice process, and demonstrates how the career-choice process can be targeted to broaden participation in computing and other STEM fields.

abstractText:
NON-TECHNICAL DESCRIPTION: Today, the means to realize active and reversible control over thermal conductivity in solid-state materials are extremely limited, despite the strong demands from both the energy and electronics industries for energy regulation. One promising strategy is to manipulate reconfigurable interfaces in materials with substantial thermal resistances to heat flow. This project advances the current fundamental understanding on the thermal transport mechanisms across these reconfigurable interfaces. This research has translational implications for a wide range of applications in the sustainable energy infrastructure, such as waste-heat energy conversion, energy harvesting, and solid-state cooling for integrated electronics. Research and education are integrated through a focus on motivating and training students to pursue science and engineering occupations, specifically in the areas of materials for sustainable energy and advanced electronics.

TECHNICAL DETAILS:  Fundamental mechanisms on how the thermal energy is transferred across reconfigurable domain walls in ferroelectric materials is poorly understood. Therefore, the focus of the project is to elucidate the roles of ferroelectric domain walls, especially their spatial distribution (e.g., density, orientation, and shape anisotropy), on the Kapitza resistance and thermal transport. Complementary theoretical and experimental approaches are applied: (1) The anisotropic thermal conductivity of ferroelectric thin films and single crystals are measured to reveal the dependence of Kapitza resistance at domain walls on the domain structures and temperature; (2) Molecular dynamics simulation is conducted to analyze how the Kapitza resistance depends on the interactions of energy carriers (i.e., phonons) with domain walls. These research activities aim to advance the current understanding on the microscopic thermal transport mechanisms in ferroelectric materials. The outreach activities are developing cinematic 360 virtual-reality laboratory tours to ‘teleport’ on-line K-12 students into the laboratory to visualize materials research and applications in sustainable energy. Undergraduate and graduate students are trained through interdisciplinary research experiences to promote the importance and challenges of energy savings, thermal management, and energy conversion in sustainable energy infrastructure.

projectOutComesReport:
Goals
The major research goal of this project was to understand how the thermal conductivity of ferroelectric materials can be switched using external electric fields through reconfigurable domain walls. We aimed to test how the spatial distribution of ferroelectric domain walls can be controlled to enable on-demand, and to elucidate the mechanisms governing thermal transport across them. The project focused on representative ferroelectric materials, including BaTiO₃, PZT, PMN-PT, and PIN-PMN-PT. The educational objective was to motivate and train students to pursue STEM careers, with emphasis on materials for sustainable energy applications.

Intellectual Merit
This project achieved significant research outcomes:

  1. Publications: We published seven peer-reviewed papers, including four in high-profile journals such as Nature Communications, Advanced Materials, Science Advances, and Advanced Science. Two papers were selected as Editor’s Picks. Four additional manuscripts are under review, with several more in preparation, reflecting the strong productivity and impact of this project.
  2. Thermal Modulation in PMN-PT: We demonstrated room-temperature thermal conductivity modulation in 2.5 mm-thick PMN-PT single crystals. By systematically studying composition and orientation dependence, we achieved a maximum thermal switching ratio of ≈1.27 in bulk materials. Optimized poling conditions generate domain-size inhomogeneity and enhance domain wall density, enabling thermal control in bulk crystals. These results confirm that thermal transport in relaxor-ferroelectrics can be tuned by manipulating mesoscale domain configurations.
  3. Room-Temperature Electrical Depoling and Repoling: We discovered that AC electric fields near the coercive field (<10 Hz) can depolarize poled PIN-PMN-PT crystals at room temperature, bypassing the need for high-temperature annealing above the Curie temperature Tc. We further demonstrated reversible polarization switching in relaxor-PT ultrasound transducers without performance degradation, supported by phase-field simulations that map the kinetics of domain evolution. This result shows that polarization states can be precisely tailored in situ, offering device designers a new approach to adaptive functionality.
  4. Universal Phonon Mean Free Path (MFP) Distribution: We grew high-quality epitaxial BaTiO₃ thin films and combined thickness-dependent thermal conductivity measurements with first-principles modeling (including four-phonon scattering) to determine the phonon MFP distribution. We found that sub-100 nm phonons dominate thermal transport, with phonons >10 nm contributing ~35% of the total thermal conductivity—contrasting earlier experimental reports. We also summarized the MFP distribution for many strongly anharmonic complex crystals and found such distribution is universal. These results improve the predictive understanding of thermal transport in strongly anharmonic crystals and provide key input for engineering nanostructures with targeted thermal performance.
  5. In-Situ Domain Wall Imaging: We developed Instant Polarized Light Microscopy (IPOLπ), a simple and robust optical technique for through-volume, single-shot observation of domain wall evolution during electric poling. Demonstrated on PIN-PMN-PT single crystals, IPOLπ enabled direct visualization of polarization dynamics, layered domain formation, and birefringence-current correlations during DC poling, AC poling, and electrical depoling. The technique’s low cost and simplicity will make it broadly adoptable by research and teaching labs.
  6. Advancing Theory: We improved computational techniques to extract full phonon dispersions and lifetimes from finite-temperature molecular dynamics simulations, enabling more accurate predictions of interfacial thermal transport. This methodology can be generalized to other complex oxides, expanding its relevance to the materials modeling community.
  7. Spin Dynamics Discovery: An unplanned outcome was the observation of anomalous spin current absorption in chiral metal oxides, leading to colossal anisotropic Gilbert damping (up to 1000% variation). This finding reveals the interplay between chirality and spin dynamics and offers new approaches for directing spin current transport in next-generation spintronic devices.

Broader Impacts

  1. Research Impact:
    Our results highlight the potential of commercially available relaxor-ferroelectric crystals for active thermal control and reveal new strategies for electric-field-driven polarization tailoring. The experimentally validated phonon MFP distribution paves the way for thermal management in nanostructured perovskite systems. IPOLπ offers a widely accessible tool for studying real-time domain wall behavior. Our discovery in spin dynamics broadens the impact beyond thermal transport to spintronic applications.
  2. Education and Training:
    This project provided hands-on research training for graduate and undergraduate students, who developed problem-solving, data analysis, and interdisciplinary collaboration skills. Students regularly presented research in group meetings, project meetings, conference talks, and posters, enhancing communication skills.
  3. Publications and Dissemination:
    We published seven peer-reviewed papers (with four more under review) and gave several conference presentations. The PIs delivered invited talks at Gordon Research Conferences (GRC), Materials Research Society (MRS), Minerals, Metals & Materials Society (TMS), IEEE, and American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) conferences, increasing the visibility of the research.
  4. Outreach:
    The team actively engaged in STEM outreach, including NCSU’s Launch Your Excellent Adventures with Physics!(LEAP) program for middle/high school girls, Science Olympiad activities, Creating Opportunities in STEM for Students with Disabilities (CATALYST), and a Kyran Anderson Academy workshop where students from nine counties designed and tested insulated containers to slow ice melting. Pre/post assessments showed measurable learning gains and strong enthusiasm for hands-on science. A 3D interactive video tour of the Nanoscale Thermal Transport Lab was developed to make research accessible to a wider audience.

abstractText:
Technologies involving robotics/automation have become prevalent in US manufacturing and service sectors.  Business leaders who adopt these technologies must prioritize cybersecurity to ensure the safety and security of their cyber-physical systems.  As a result, the interrelated areas of robotics/automation and cybersecurity are vital to US manufacturers.  This project will create an Advanced Technological Education (ATE) Coordination Network that includes community colleges with active ATE projects, Manufacturing Extension Partnerships, Manufacturing USA Institutes, and the National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education.  The goal of this Coordination Network is to increase members’ understanding of the knowledge and skills required to operate and maintain connected machines securely in a manufacturing setting.

Through workshops, virtual communication, and other modalities, this Coordination Network intends to facilitate the sharing of best practices about how to develop community college students’ knowledge and skills in robotics/automation and cybersecurity.  It will also promote awareness of organizations and resources that connect students to work-based learning opportunities. This Coordination Network will connect community college students to potential employers in the Manufacturing Extension Parternships client base.  By establishing connections and nurturing relationships among members, it is expected that the efforts of the Coordination Network will create synergies that magnify and broaden the impact of individual efforts.  The Coordination Network's web portal will make education and training materials available to non-members.  This project is funded by the Advanced Technological Education program that focuses on the education of technicians for the advanced-technology fields that drive the nation's economy.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
The main outcome of this coordination network project was the network itself.  Those engaged in the network include community college faculty and administrators, Manufacturing Extension Partnership (MEP) representatives, workforce development officers from two Manufacturing USA Innovation Institutes, and the director of the National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education (NICE).  While the project focused on developing technician training at the convergence of robotics/automation and cybersecurity, building this training by engaging individuals from these organizations enabled the enhancement of relationships between community colleges and MEPs across seven states.  It also led to several new partnerships and collaborations across coordination network members.

A second outcome of the project was the development of a micro-credential called the Cyber4RAM (RAM = robotics/automation/mechatronics) digital badge.  This micro-credential is available via a no-fee learning management system, making it accessible to all US learners.  The 11 modules of the micro-credential are focused on 11 of the NICE competencies that tie back to advanced manufacturing.  The goal of the micro-credential is to build cyber awareness among technicians working in robotics/automation/mechatronics.  More information on the Cyber4RAM digital badge (micro-credential) is available here: https://ncmep.org/tracks-cn/badge/.

In terms of broader impacts, the network itself has impacted learners across seven states (NC, SC, IL, MI, VA, PA, OH) via new collaborations with industry and with others in the coordination network.  Additionally, the micro-credential has been earned by 97 learners, potentially better positioning them for employment in advanced manufacturing.  Participation by two of the Manufacturing USA Innovation Institutes provided all coordination network members with opportunities to learn more about the Manufacturing USA program and to potentially partner with an Institute on a grant or other collaborative effort.

abstractText:
This project aims to serve the national interest by increasing the diversity of the STEM workforce of the United States. To do so, the project proposes to increase students’ perception of, interest in, and motivation to pursue research careers. Research studies have shown that students, particularly women, students from historically underserved groups, and first-generation students, often value communal goals of working together and helping people.  Consequently, the project proposes to create innovative undergraduate courses in which students not only perform STEM research but also apply their research work to directly serve their communities. This combination of research and service learning has the potential to transform students’ ideas about research, including the capacity of research to help people.  In addition, it can also empower the communities with whom the students work.

We propose to combine two high-impact practices, service learning and research experiences, to create a Service-Learning theme within a Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experience (SL-CURE).  This SL-CURE will be implemented in three different institutions: (1) a large, public, historically black university; (2) a small, private, predominantly white liberal arts college; and (3) a large, public Hispanic serving institution in the context of multiple disciplines (biology, public health, social work). Assessing the impact of the SL-CURE will be grounded in the theory of the transtheoretical stages of change from pre-contemplation (when students don’t consider research as a potential career) through preparation (when students develop scientific skills and a broader, more realistic perspective of research affordance of communal goals). The project will also contribute to the STEM education community by assessing how specific implementations of service-learning, including community-based participatory research, science communication and outreach, and mentoring, influence students’ perceptions of, interest in, and engagement in research practices not only during the course, but also one to two years beyond course completion. Disseminating this model is expected to influence existing and future CURES, which may result in a strong positive impact on retaining diverse individuals in the STEM workforce pipeline. This project is supported by the NSF Improving Undergraduate STEM Education Program: Education and Human Resources.   The IUSE: EHR program supports research and development projects to improve the effectiveness of STEM education for all students. This project is in the Engaged Student Learning track, through which the program supports the creation, exploration, and implementation of promising practices and tools.

projectOutComesReport:
​​Rationale/hypothesis: There is significant disparity between STEM workforce demographics and the diversity of the United States as historically underserved populations remain underrepresented in the scientific and technological workforce. One potential cause of this disparity is a discrepancy between the students' perception of the goals attainable through research and their own personal and professional goals. This inconsistency potentially originates from misconceptions of the scientific endeavor, often misrepresented as individualistic and detached from community issues. In an effort to illustrate how scientific inquiry can serve communal as well as agentic (individualistic) goals, we designed a courses that combined two high-impact practices at multiple institutions:

●  Service learning (SL) - an educational approach that integrates community engagement with academic coursework allowing students to apply classroom knowledge to real world challenges while reciprocally benefiting the community, promoting hands-on learning and civic responsibility.

●  Course based Undergraduate research Experiences (CUREs)-  educational programs that integrate authentic research activities into undergraduate coursework. Unlike traditional labs with known outcomes, CUREs engage students in authentic research, allowing them to contribute to scientific discovery.

We hypothesized that combining service learning with course-based undergraduate research experiences (SL-CUREs) would enhance underrepresented students' interest in STEM by changing students’ perceptions of careers in STEM research as a way to achieve both their communal and agentic goals. 

Methodology:  Working at diverse institutions ranging from large public minority serving universities to small, private colleges, we designed courses where students participated in authentic research. The CURE projects varied between institutions, including: (1) the collection and characterization of plants and invertebrate species in restoration sites, (2) the isolation of new antibiotic-producing soil bacteria, (3) analysis of water quality in residential homes, (4) assessment of the impact of mobile food markets on health and behavior of individuals in regions designated as food deserts, and (5) molecular genetics analysis of ecologically important gopher tortoises. In conjunction with some of these CUREs, we incorporated service learning, where students engaged in civic projects related to the research studies. These included: (1) Ecological restoration service, (2) work with food distribution centers and mobile markets to serve food insecure communities, (3) Educational programming on water quality for North Carolina middle/high schools. In order to assess the impact of SL-CURES on student perceptions and career goals, we collected and analyzed a combination of both quantitative and qualitative data from Pre and Post assessment surveys (goal orientation and goal affordance) as well as short (21) and long-term (29) interviews.

Intellectual Merit: We observed unexpected results in goal orientation across student groups who varied in their communal and agentic goals. Although all students hold both communal and agentic goal orientations, those hailing from minoritized groups hold more communal-oriented goals. Given the discrepancies between our data and the current literature regarding goal orientation, we developed a new assessment tool: Goal Affordance Priority Sorting Exercise (GAPSE). This innovative tool uses a venn diagram format where students sort goals into categories that reflect either their personal importance, their alignment with research, or both. This tool provides insight into the motivations and perceptions of students, particularly students from underserved communities who may view research careers as less aligned with their communal goals. Researchers and educators can use this tool to develop interventions that target misconceptions about research as well as to help highlight types of research that can help students fulfill personal goals, thus removing a barrier for minoritized individuals entering research. Most existing analyses of CUREs analyze within course changes. Our long-term interviews revealed that both CURE and SL-CURE courses increased students’ interest in research and inspired future engagement in additional research-based courses and independent research experiences, partly because students were exposed to a variety of research topics that expanded their view of what research is and how research can solve problems. These insights inform the construction of more equitable learning environments that can promote the academic success of all STEM students. 

Broader Impact: Our project provided students from underrepresented backgrounds with meaningful research and service-learning experiences.  In addition, the research project also provided training and professional development opportunities for both undergraduate and graduate students on methodologies in educational research, including the completion of a master’s thesis and doctoral dissertation. Dissemination of findings include multiple poster presentations and invited conference presentations at national education conferences including SABER, Gordon Research Conference, SEISMIC. Further, peer-reviewed manuscripts detailing our findings are in progress for publication at leading educational journals. Ultimately, continuation of this work, including scaling up SL-CUREs and further assessment of the impact on diverse student populations is planned, with the goal of broadening participation and inclusion to strengthen the STEM workforce by bringing a wide range of perspectives and ideas necessary to tackle complex scientific and technological challenges.

abstractText:
Pollution from past releases of toxic organic contaminants continue to plague the Nation’s water, soil, and sediment. While various technologies and approaches have been developed to remediate these legacy pollutants, they continue to present challenges for communities around the country. The overall goal of this CAREER project is to address these challenges and protect human and the environmental health by developing treatment technologies that more completely degrade toxic organic pollutants in a cost-effective manner. The basis for this technology is a hybrid microbial-material process. In this approach, microorganisms provide the driving force to enable reactions on the surface of materials that degrade the organic pollutant. While this process has shown great promise, there are many gaps in our knowledge of how this process occurs. The fundamental insight gained will permit the informed design and optimization of materials that can degrade specific pollutants. These materials can then be applied to engineered systems such as water and wastewater treatment plants. The integrated education plan will have significant and broad impacts and will reach a diverse audience of K-12 teachers and students through a mentoring program for underrepresented high school students in partnership with the NC School of Science and Mathematics. These efforts will increase the scientific literacy of the Nation and help develop the STEM workforce of the future.

The overall goal of this CAREER project is to study the fundamental mechanisms of how microbial-driven electron transfer from redox-active materials transform organic contaminants. Conventional methods for the biological treatment of organic contaminants like chlorinated solvents rely on the activity of specific bacteria. These bacteria are often low in abundance and sparsely distributed in the subsurface, and materials that harness the activity of these bacteria can greatly enhance and sustain contaminant removal. Geobacter, a group of bacteria that are present in water, soil, and sediment are extremely metabolically versatile in their ability to utilize insoluble electron acceptors such as pyrogenic carbonaceous materials (PCMs). Geobacter use PCMs such as activated carbon and biochar to shuttle electrons through the material to abiotically degrade contaminants on the material surface. The PI will combine the tools of electrochemistry, microscopy, spectroscopy, and molecular biology to address knowledge gaps in our understanding of these interactions at microbial-material-contaminant interfaces. Three complimentary goals in the proposed program will be pursued: (1) Determine the role of PCM properties on microbial and contaminant reactivity, (2) Assess the role of contaminant adsorption on reaction kinetics and toxicity to the microorganisms, and (3) Determine the effect of environmental matrix components on the resiliency of reactions mediated by PCMs. With this information, a new generation of materials can be designed to degrade organic pollutants in applications including drinking water, stormwater, and bioremediation systems. The research objectives will be integrated with innovative education initiatives. K-12 teachers in biology will learn advanced microscopy and experiment kits to introduce students to environmental microbiology. Collaboration with the Friday Institute for Educational Innovation will leverage these activities to reach hundreds of K-12 teachers and students through existing school partnerships with the annual NC Science Teachers Association Conference. A multi-level mentoring program for underrepresented high school students will be piloted at the NC School of Science and Mathematics to provide research experiences to help students pursue careers in STEM. Finally, a new undergraduate-level lab on PCM microbial reactivity at will be developed at NCSU.

abstractText:
Most insects carry bacteria that live within their cells; these bacteria are inherited from their mothers. The bacteria may manipulate their insect hosts’ reproduction in ways that improves the health or number of female hosts carrying the bacterium. Relevant to this study, these bacterial “symbionts” can sabotage host sperm such that fertilized eggs laid by females without the bacterium die early in life (“cytoplasmic incompatibility,” or “CI”). Currently, two common, unrelated bacteria are known to cause CI in insects: Wolbachia, and Cardinium hertigii, the focus of this study. The main goal of this project is to discover the molecular mechanism by which Cardinium causes CI in insects. The benefits of this work are at least two-fold. Bacteria such as Cardinium target animal cell division, a fundamental process that can be understood better when examining how Cardinium interferes with it. Secondly, CI-causing bacteria may be used for pest or vector management. The CI agent Wolbachia reduces the susceptibility to viruses of insects that carry it, and is currently being introduced around the world to mosquito populations, with major implications for reduction of vector-borne disease and the global bioeconomy. The project will also provide engaging science education targeted for under-represented groups through outreach programs for elementary school (U Arizona Insect Discovery and Insect Festival), high school (production of a book “Animal Manipulating Parasites at NC State, and Iowa State George Washington Carver Internship program) and undergraduate students (via research opportunities at all three institutions). 

For Cardinium strains that infect Encarsia spp., parasitic wasps of whiteflies, genomic and transcriptomic studies have identified candidate genes that are likely to be important in CI and/or symbiosis. The central hypotheses are that (1) Cardinium effector proteins involved in modifying host DNA during spermatogenesis are associated with the testes, and other Cardinium effectors involved with rescue of modified sperm are present in the ovaries of infected wasps, (2) the role of these proteins can be inferred by identifying the host proteins they interact with and (3) that the B vitamin biotin has a critical role in CI and/or the symbiosis. The project presents a unique opportunity to test these hypotheses with a diverse array of approaches, in four objectives: (1) Compare Cardinium localization and CI candidate gene expression in male pupal Encarsia, the “modification” stage, with patterns observed in adults.(2) Identify Cardinium and Encarsia proteins involved in CI with differential proteomics. (3) Use heterologous expression to identify interacting host proteins of CI candidate proteins. (4) Investigate the role of Cardinium synthesized biotin in modification of host proteins. This project will shed light on the sophisticated CI reproductive manipulation by Cardinium. Cardinium has received comparatively little attention, but produces a virtually identical CI phenotype to Wolbachia with what appears to be completely independent eukaryote-interacting genes, a plasmid and not a phage, and an unusual type 6 secretion system. What is learned about Cardinium candidate gene function, expression and host targets will illuminate CI and symbiosis in both systems.

projectOutComesReport:
Many insects carry bacteria that are inherited from their mothers. These symbiotic bacteria live within the insects’ cells. Several symbiotic bacteria manipulate their insect hosts’ reproduction in ways that favors their transmission to the next generation. Some of these symbionts sabotage host sperm such that fertilized eggs laid by females without the bacterium die early in life (“cytoplasmic incompatibility,” or “CI”). In this interaction, eggs that contain the bacterium are able to “rescue” the sperm and normal development occurs. Of the six bacteria known to cause CI, Wolbachia is best studied, and genes involved in causing CI in Wolbachia have been discovered. Cardinium hertigii, the focus of this project, causes CI without the same genes Wolbachia uses. The overall goal of this proposal was to discover the genes involved in CI in Cardinium.

We analyzed the localization of two different CI-causing Cardinium strains in the reproductive tract of pupae and adult Encarsia wasps and found that the two different Cardinium strains show distinct patterns in where they are found in the reproductive tract. Further, the finding that sperm development is complete by the end of the pupal stage indicated that pupal males should be examined for Cardinium protein expression.

We developed a protein sequence database for both the symbiont and the host, critical for protein identification. This database will also be highly valuable beyond this project as a reference for other scientists working with Encarsia wasps.

We detected Cardinium proteins in whole pupal and adult Encarsia wasps and in Encarsia tissues such as ovaries and testes. Among the proteins detected, five were most abundant and showed expression patterns that were indicative of being potentially involved in CI.

These five proteins were cloned and expressed in yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) to investigate if these proteins have a toxic effect on yeast cells. We reasoned that a protein secreted by Cardinium into sperm may serve as a toxin during early cell division of the embryo if no Cardinium are present in the egg to neutralize the toxin. Since cell division in yeast is similar to cell division in animals we used yeast cells to test if expression of suspected Cardinium toxin proteins would lead to toxicity in yeast. Out of those five proteins, one (CAHE_0406) resulted in a toxic effect when expressed in yeast cells. Homologs of this protein in other Cardinium strains that were similar (but not identical), did not show a toxic effect to yeast cells. A protein encoded by the gene adjacent to CAHE_0406, CAHE_0405, was detected in pupal testes in much lower quantities than CAHE_0406. This gene did not have a toxic effect on yeast and is currently being evaluated as a possible “rescue” or “antidote” gene.

Broader Impacts

As part of the project, Dr. Eleanor Spicer-Rice, together with the project team, developed a book about microbes and animals for middle school age student and the book was picked up by MIT Kids Press, an imprint of the well-established children’s publisher Candlewick Press. The book was released in May 2023 and has been very successful. It is titled “Unseen Jungle: The Microbes That Secretly Control Our World”. The book features many engaging stories on the important and weird things that microbes do particularly in interaction with animals and plants. Additionally, the book features five interviews with scientists from diverse backgrounds including an interview with the PI Martha (Molly) Hunter.

The project also supported several other training and outreach activities. The PhD student employed in the Hunter laboratory as a graduate student and first year postdoc went on to complete a postdoc and is now transitioning to a tenure track faculty position. Two graduate students have been supported in the Schmitz-Esser and Kleiner laboratory and have completed or are completing first authored manuscripts. Five undergraduates were employed on the project in the Hunter laboratory, two in the Schmitz-Esser laboratory and three in the Kleiner laboratory. The Schmitz-Esser lab hosted two Hispanic high school students through the Iowa State University Science Bound Internship program for underrepresented groups for a six-week summer internship. Hunter and the graduate student in the Hunter laboratory both participated for multiple years in the Arizona Insect Festival, a one-day outreach event to the local community which attracts between three and five thousand people, mostly families, to engage in exhibits and activities showcasing research on insects and insect diversity. They also both participated in Insect Discovery, a semester long series of interactive workshops about insect diversity and behavior for elementary school children.

abstractText:
NON-TECHNICAL DESCRIPTION: The goal of this research project is to develop synthesis and processing routes to optimize the efficacy of titania-based nanoparticles for inactivating SARS-CoV-2 surrogate coronaviruses. The chemistry and stoichiometry of titania particles are tuned through a novel flow-synthesis processing route and subsequent thermal annealing to make the material photoactive in the visible-light range of the electromagnetic spectrum. Such light activation leads to the production of reactive oxygen species, which are believed to be central to the antiviral activity of such oxide materials. Being able to control and optimize the antiviral activity of materials such as titania, which can easily be coated onto surfaces or integrated into fibers, can have direct and immediate impact on the production of antimicrobial coatings and personal protective equipment (PPE). As such, the research results are proactively directed towards groups researching and developing PPE materials for the COVID-19 pandemic. The graduate students involved in the research are team-mentored in a highly interdisciplinary and societally relevant research activity that spans materials research, photochemistry, virology, and materials manufacturing.

TECHNICAL DETAILS: This research program aims to develop the fundamental science linking the chemistry of titanium dioxide, or titania, to its antiviral properties. The research is motivated by the urgent need to develop coatings and personal protective equipment (PPE) that can inactivate the COVID-19 virus.  In this research, precise synthesis of titania nanoparticles is achieved via a micro-scale flow synthesis platform with in situ diagnostics. The high-throughput experimental platform enables the research team to study systematically the important variables of particle size, phase, and doping concentrations on the light absorption and photodynamic properties of titania. An important variable in the study is oxygen stoichiometry, which is systematically controlled through low-partial-pressure oxygen annealing. The reduction reaction induces oxygen vacancies into the titania lattice, which, in turn, lower the optical band gap of the material. The consequences for reactive oxygen species generation, which are critical for antiviral efficacy, have not, however, previously been established. Therefore, this research measures the effects of nanoparticle stoichiometry on the generation of individual reactive oxygen species: superoxide, singlet oxygen, hydrogen peroxide and hydroxyl radicals under visible light illumination. Finally, the efficacy for inactivating SARS-CoV-2 surrogate coronaviruses is assessed, allowing for the development of full synthesis-structure-property-function relationships for this important antimicrobial photodynamic material. Moreover, the research translates the knowledge and processing conditions of the most efficacious materials to groups producing antiviral materials for the COVID-19 crisis. The participating graduate students are involved in all aspects of this highly interdisciplinary research activity, which provides them unique experience in the material design process, while contributing to practical solutions for the containment of the COVID-19 virus.

projectOutComesReport:
The COVID-19 pandemic put a spotlight on the need for antimicrobial materials, not just specifically against the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, but for other pathogens (e.g., hospital acquired infections) as well. Functional antimicrobial materials with self-disinfecting properties will play an increasingly important role over the coming years for pandemic prevention. This research program established copper-doped titania (TiO2) as an efficacious material to inactivate several viral and bacterial strains in the presence of visible light. While titania is known to have desirable antimicrobial properties, this is normally only achieved in ultra-violet radiation.  By controlled doping of titania with copper ions, we were able to shift the activity to visible light wavelengths.  The program also showed that the titania materials could be incorporated into a polymer host and spray coated onto a solid surface, while remaining active as an antiviral material.

In addition to the positive scientific outcomes related to virus and bacteria deactivation and the potential for improving public heath, the research program also provided a unique highly interdisciplinary research environment for five graduate students.  The research team worked to bring their various disciplinary expertise to address a critical need for developing virucidal materials that are not only efficacious as photodynamic materials for virus inactivation, but which can also be manufactured and integrated into engineering products.  This focused, performance-driven program was a unique training environment for all researchers involved.

abstractText:
When individuals lose a lower limb, they rely on a prosthesis to restore their basic mobility in daily living.  But most modern robotic prosthetic legs operate autonomously, without direct communication with the user, which limits the functionality and versatility of these assistive devices.  This project will develop a novel bi-directional neural-machine interface that enables individuals with lower limb amputations to operate and sense their prosthetic leg intuitively and naturally.  Project outcomes will have profound societal impact by improving the mobility and stability, balance confidence, and overall quality of life for the large community of individuals with lower limb amputation, while alleviating phantom pain.  In the longer term, the technology created by this research may lead to a paradigm shift in the commercial development of medical assistive devices other than prostheses.  In addition, undergraduate and graduate students in neural and rehabilitation engineering will be trained as members of the research team, and K-12 students from underrepresented groups will be engaged through educational and outreach activities.

This research will develop a novel non-invasive and bi-directional neural-machine interface (NMI) for a bionic prosthetic ankle that enables seamless integration of robotic prostheses and their users for improved mobility and stability.  The project will encompass three main thrusts: investigation of high-density transcutaneous nerve stimulation and new encoding algorithms for evoking the illusion of sensation in an amputated foot (a sensory interface); development of novel EMG decoding algorithms based on machine learning and neurophysiological modeling approaches for continuous neural control of a prosthetic ankle (a motor interface); and design and fabrication of a bidirectional NMI that combines both of the aforementioned sensory and motor interfaces to achieve embodied integration of a prosthetic ankle within the user.  The NMI prototype will be validated on individuals with transtibial amputations when performing various activities common in daily living.

projectOutComesReport:
Project Summary

Individuals with lower-limb amputations rely on prostheses to stay active in daily life. However, current commercial robotic prostheses operate autonomously, without direct communication between the device and the user, which limits their adaptability and functionality. Through this Cyber-Human Systems (CHS) award, we developed a novel bi-directional human–machine interface that enables individuals with transtibial amputations to both control and perceive their prosthetic leg in a more intuitive and natural manner.

Research Achievement

This CHS project has led to the following technological innovations and scientific contributions:

  1. Neural control framework for robotic prosthetic ankles

We developed a neurophysiological model–based approach to decode neuromuscular control signals, electromyography (EMG), for muscle force prediction and continuous neural control of a prosthetic ankle. To demonstrate the benefits of neural prosthesis control, we focused on tasks that are difficult for autonomous control systems, such as anticipatory postural adjustments. Our results showed that neurally controlled prosthetic ankles shifted users’ postural and neuromuscular control strategies toward those observed in non-disabled individuals.

  1. High-density haptic feedback interfaces for sensory restoration

We designed and tested two high-density (HD) haptic feedback interfaces to restore plantar haptic perception or ankle proprioception in prosthesis users: (1) transcutaneous nerve stimulation and (2) a haptics vest. We found that while HD transcutaneous electrical stimulation can elicit plantar pressure sensations, it is highly sensitive to electrode placement, posing challenges for daily use. In contrast, the HD haptics vest is flexible, programmable, and capable of substituting lost sensations by providing intuitive discrete or continuous feedback.

  1. Closed-loop control of bionic ankles

We integrated the HD haptics vest (afferent interface) with EMG-based neural control (efferent interface), allowing individuals with transtibial amputations to operate a bionic leg in a closed-loop manner. This closed-loop system enabled users to perform ankle position-matching tasks more accurately and generate higher push-off torques during walking than when using efferent control alone.

Broader Impacts and Dissemination

The concepts and technologies developed in this project have been widely disseminated. The project has resulted in 12 peer-reviewed journal papers and 4 conference papers published in high-impact venues such as Science Robotics, IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering, and IEEE Transactions on Haptics. Our Science Robotics publication was featured in multiple news outlets, including the NSF website (https://news.ncsu.edu/2023/10/robotic-ankles-move-naturally/)

Over the past five years, this CHS award and its RUE supplements have provided research opportunities for 7 graduate students, 14 undergraduate students, and 2 postdoctoral fellows. Four graduate students completed their training and have since continued in academia (e.g., NIH) or joined high-tech R&D companies (e.g., DEKA R&D Corp). Additionally, our outreach activities have promoted STEM and human-centered computing to over 200 K–12 students, and this effort will continue beyond the duration of the grant.

The project has also fostered new collaborations, including a partnership with the prosthetics company Össur (Iceland). Building upon the technologies developed, we have initiated a clinical trial to translate our findings into clinical practice. We strongly believe that the outcomes of this project will have a lasting impact by paving the way toward restoring mobility, independence, and an improved quality of life for people with lower-limb amputations.
